`CONTRIBUTING.md`:

```md
# Contributing to Hermes Hook

Thank you for your interest in Hermes Hook. Bug reports, reports on games that work or fail, ideas and pull requests are all welcome.

## Reporting bugs

Please use the [bug report form](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/issues/new/choose). The most helpful attachment is the ZIP from **Log → Export bug report …** in Hermes: it contains the activity log, the log and `crash.log`.

Look through the ZIP before you attach it: issues are public, and the logs contain file paths (with your user name) and the names of the processes you attached to. Values from the game's memory are not in it.

Security problems go through a private report instead, see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## Before a larger change

For anything bigger than a small fix, please open an issue first and describe what you have in mind. This avoids work on something that does not fit the project or is already in progress.

Not accepted are contributions that aim at online or multiplayer games, bypass anti-cheat systems or hide Hermes from them.

## Development setup

Python 3.11 or newer is needed. On Linux, the tests and Hermes itself need `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0`.

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
./.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[test,docs]"
./.venv/bin/python -m pytest
```

Many tests compile a small C program and attach to it with Frida; they are skipped without `gcc`, with a different `ptrace_scope` or on machines other than x86-64. The [development documentation](docs/development/index.md) explains the test targets, the [architecture](docs/development/architecture.md) and how the documentation and its screenshots are built.

## Pull requests

- Keep a pull request to one topic and base it on `main`.
- Add or update tests for changed behaviour, and run `pytest` before you push.
- Comments, docstrings, documentation and commit messages are in English. Commit messages start with a verb in the imperative ("Add …", "Fix …").
- UI texts go into both `hermes/ui/localization/en.json` and `de.json`. If you do not speak German, add the English text to both and say so in the pull request.
- Icons are Google Material Icons (Outlined), stored in `hermes/ui/resources/icons/`.
- Update the documentation in `docs/` when you change what users see, and check it with `mkdocs build --strict`.
- Do not commit files extracted from games (assemblies, assets, dumps). They are not ours to publish.

## License

Hermes Hook is published under the [MIT License](LICENSE). By submitting a contribution, you agree that it is published under the same license.

```

A. HISTORY OF THE SOFTWARE

Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting
Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands
as a successor of a language called ABC.  Guido remains Python's
principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.

In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for

`README.md`:

```md
# Hermes Hook

Hermes Hook is a desktop application for inspecting and manipulating the memory of running games. It runs on Linux, including Windows games under Wine/Proton, and on Windows. The project is under development.

The full documentation with screenshots is in [`docs/`](docs/index.md); `mkdocs serve` shows it as a website (see [Development](docs/development/index.md#documentation)).

## Disclaimer

This tool is intended solely for educational, research, and single-player game modding purposes. It is not designed or intended to bypass anti-cheat mechanisms or be used in online multiplayer games. The developer assumes no responsibility or liability for any account bans, suspensions, or damages resulting from the use or misuse of this software.

Use of the feature for restoring memory modifications may be detected by anti-tamper systems (such as Arxan) and, when used online, will inevitably result in account bans or soft bans. Use it at your own risk.

## Features

- **Memory scan** for integers and floats, with follow-up scans, tolerance and rounded floats
- **Tracked addresses** with live values, writing and freezing
- **Pointer scan** that finds the value again after the game restarts
- **Write and read watch**: which code writes or reads an address
- **Hooks** on write instructions: multiply, fix, clamp or compute values in JavaScript, reinstalled at every start
- **Hook templates**, testable without a game, and a debug window for hooks
- **Scripts** that call game code on a schedule or by hand
- **Native trace and function monitor** for any engine
- **Unity (Mono and IL2CPP) and Unreal Engine**: catalog of classes and methods, trace, method monitor, object inspector, method hooks and calls; GAS attributes for Unreal
- **Wine and Proton** support through Frida's Windows gadget
- Memory viewer, sessions, activity log, export and import per game, color themes, German and English

## Quick start

Python 3.11 or newer is needed. In the project directory:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
./.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .
./.venv/bin/hermes
```

On Linux, Hermes needs `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0` to access a game started separately. The [installation guide](docs/getting-started/installation.md), the [permissions](docs/getting-started/permissions.md) and a [tutorial](docs/getting-started/first-hook.md) with the test game in `test_app/` have the details.

## License

Copyright (C) 2026 Frank Hoogen

Hermes Hook is distributed under the MIT License. It is provided without any warranty; see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

The third-party components and their licenses are listed in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES); the full license texts are in [LICENSES](LICENSES/).

```

`ROADMAP.md`:

```md
# Roadmap and ideas

Extensions that would help find addresses and hook entry points, and open points from the
work so far. As of November 2026.

What Hermes can do today is described in the [documentation](docs/index.md); what was learned
while building it is in the [implementation notes](docs/development/implementation-notes.md).

## Proposals, independent of any engine

Sorted by benefit relative to effort.

### 1. Native call diff trace: follow-ups

The native trace and the native function monitor exist (see the
[documentation](docs/guide/native-tools.md)). Open:

- Try it in a real native Linux game (load, playability, quality of the hits).
- The 32-bit path of the native trace under Wine is untested (Shadowrun Returns is Mono, where
  native tools ask first: they crashed it).
- Callers: the sequence shows the call site of the first call per thread. A list of all
  callers per function (a count per call site and target) is still missing.
- A disassembler view and a hook on a function found in the trace; update-proof byte
  signatures are point 5.
- Threads created during the trace are not followed.
- The native function monitor has not been tried in Baldur's Gate (native, Linux) yet.

### 2. "Which addresses does this instruction touch?"

The reverse of the write watch: hook the write instruction that was found and collect all
the addresses it accesses, each with registers and caller.

- Solves the problem of **shared code**: the same instruction lowers the HP of the player
  *and* the enemies. The comparison shows which address belongs to the player and how the
  code tells them apart (register, caller, team field).
- The hook agent can already read registers and build caller signatures.

### 3. Dissecting and comparing structures

Once an address is known, the surrounding object is of interest: max HP, mana, gold and team
usually lie next to it.

- **Structure view:** interpret memory from the start of the object as fields (pointers,
  floats, ints, strings) with a guessed type. For Mono objects the object inspector already
  shows the fields with their types and offsets; native memory has nothing like it yet.
- **Instance comparison:** player against enemy, or two points in time side by side, with
  the differences highlighted
- **Reverse search:** who points to this object? Leads to the base pointer and to stable
  pointer chains.

### 4. Entry points through strings, RTTI and symbols

- **String references:** find texts such as "Not enough gold" or "GoldAmount" in memory,
  then the code locations that refer to them. That often yields the right function directly.
- **C++ RTTI:** type names (MSVC `.?AV…@@`, Itanium `typeinfo`) lead to vtables, i.e. to
  class names for objects in memory. An address then becomes "`CPlayerStats`+0x48".
- **Symbols:** native Linux games are often not fully stripped. The native trace and monitor
  already use exported and debug symbols (`DebugSymbol`); the scanner, watch and hooks still
  show `module+0x…`.

### 5. Update-proof hooks through byte signatures

For native code, build a pattern (AOB) from the bytes around the write instruction, with
wildcards for addresses and offsets, and search for it again automatically after a game
update. For JIT code the method identity already does this; for native games it is missing.

### 6. Register hooks at any code address

Today a hook needs a write instruction: it relocates the write and hands old and new value
to the transform. Some values are better changed elsewhere, before they are written:

- **Write sites that cannot be hooked:** in Dark Souls III the souls are stored by a tiny
  setter (`mov [rcx+0x74], eax; ret` at `DarkSoulsIII.exe+0x465f13`), too short for the 5-byte
  jump. The short jump needs int3 padding nearby, which Arxan overwrites at run time, and Arxan
  restores the setter's code anyway (see the
  [implementation notes](docs/development/implementation-notes.md#write-hooks-under-anti-tamper-protection)).
- **The value is computed before it is stored:** the native function monitor showed at the
  return address `+0x5a5436` in the caller: `rax` = new souls, `rbx` = souls gained,
  `rsi` = old souls. A hook there could set `rax = rsi + rbx * factor` before the setter runs.

Proposal: a hook type on any instruction (not only writes) whose script gets the registers
(`ctx.regs.rax`, …, also flags and xmm if needed) and may change them before the instruction
runs; optionally memory through `ctx.read`/`ctx.write`.

- Reuses the trampoline of the write hooks (relocation, saved registers, short jump), the
  caller learning, the debug window and saving as module + offset
- Created from the native function monitor (call site or return address of a logged call, with
  the registers seen there) and from the disassembler view
- Templates in the same system as value templates (`kind: "registers"`), e.g. "scale register
  difference": `rax = rsi + (rax - rsi) * factor`
- Open: write back the registers from the block of the trampoline (today they are only read);
  instructions that cannot be relocated (`rip`-relative jumps are handled by Frida's relocator)

### 7. Smaller additions to the search

- **Group search:** several values at fixed distances, e.g. HP 120 and max HP 150 four bytes
  further on. Finds structures at once.
- **Save game diff:** compare two save games to recognise values and layout, then search
  memory for them.

### 8. Hooks: remaining JavaScript paths

The C fast path handles most hooked writes (see the implementation notes). Still in
JavaScript:

- On Linux, callers are checked in JavaScript (no `GetCurrentThreadStackLimits`).
- A fixed-address hook that learns callers.

### Recommendation

**2 (accesses of an instruction)** is the next larger step independent of any engine and uses
much of what exists. Among the adapters, the call graph from Blueprint bytecode is left for
**Unreal**, and the call dialog for **IL2CPP**.

## Engines

The adapter layer is described in the [architecture](docs/development/architecture.md#adding-an-engine).

### More adapters

| Engine | Approach | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | ClassDB / object properties | scene tree and variables |
| **Lua engines** | hook the `lua_*` API | tables and variables of the script state |
| **RPG Maker MV/MZ, Ren'Py** | JavaScript or Python runtime | game variables directly in the script state |

### Unreal: open

- Call graph from Blueprint bytecode (`UStruct::Script`).
- Monitor gaps: `EX_LocalOutVariable` (needs `FFrame::OutParms`) and nested expressions show
  as `?`; FText, TMap, TSet and delegates show their type only.
- The trace's callers could use the FFrame stack scan of the monitor.
- Call method: TArray, TMap, TSet, FText, delegates and structs of structs cannot be typed in.
- A trusted code-plugin interface for games with non-standard GAS setters. The agent has no
  external plugin loader; a setter with a genuinely different signature or call sequence needs
  code, not just another method name in configuration.
- UE4 before 4.23 (`TNameEntryArray` instead of `FNamePool`) and 32-bit games are not
  supported.

### IL2CPP: open

- The **Call method** dialog. Unity calls `il2cpp_runtime_invoke` on the main thread about
  17,000 times a second (also on job threads, to be filtered out), so the Mono way of running
  work on the main thread carries over. Arguments: IL2CPP passes a hidden `MethodInfo*` last.
- The call graph would need disassembly instead of IL.
- ECS games run most gameplay as Burst code (530 of 538 `OnUpdate` methods in V Rising), with
  their data in ECS chunks rather than objects; method hooks do not see it.

## Wine and Proton: open points

- **Method monitor and method hooks under Wine:** arguments follow the platform's calling
  convention (System V, Win64, x86). Still to check on a real game: Win64 with Kathy Rain 2,
  x86 with Shadowrun Returns, especially methods with structs and floats. Under 32 bit, float
  results (st0) and 64-bit results (edx:eax) are read but cannot be replaced.
- **Large traces under Wine:** with tens of thousands of methods the game froze while
  compiling (Mono's garbage collector hung in `SuspendThread`) or crashed while hooking in
  Frida's code (a write to the header of `OPENGL32.dll` at `0x7BEB0000`). Worked around with
  preselection filters and a limit (the `wine_trace_limit` setting), not fixed. A candidate
  for a bug report to Frida with a minidump.
- **32-bit Wine games:** the watch and hooks take ptrace, because the hook engine only handles
  x64 code (`installSite`).
- **Steam Linux Runtime:** a real Steam game in the container (Kathy Rain 2) is untested. The
  Windows helper runs outside the container and needs the shared `/tmp` and `/dev/shm`. If
  that fails, `nsenter` into the game's namespaces would be the next step.
- **Gadget loader (ptrace, fallback):** catches a thread with a software breakpoint at a
  frequently called Windows function (message pump, timing). Games that call none of these
  functions need `hot_points` of their own; `load_gadget` takes them, but neither the UI nor
  the settings can set them yet.

## Activity log: open

- The ptrace backends (watch, hooks) only report the start and end of the session, no single
  steps.

## Binary distribution (PyInstaller) and licenses

Open, nothing is built yet. Hermes Hook is MIT-licensed; a frozen bundle contains
third-party code whose licenses add duties that a source release through pip does not have:

- **Qt (LGPL-3.0):** users must be able to replace the bundled Qt libraries with their own
  build. Build in one-folder mode (`--onedir`), not `--onefile`, so the Qt shared libraries
  stay separate, replaceable files. Ship the LGPL text and point to the source of the exact Qt
  version (`download.qt.io`), or offer it in writing.
- **PySide6 (LGPL-3.0-only, GPL-2.0-only or GPL-3.0-only):** the Qt for Python bindings offer
  an LGPL route as well as GPL and commercial terms. A frozen bundle must meet the chosen
  license's obligations; the project's own MIT license remains unchanged.
- **License files in the bundle:** PyInstaller does not collect `LICENSE`, `LICENSES/` and
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES`; add them as data files, next to the executable.
- **Inventory the bundle:** PyInstaller pulls in more than `requirements.txt` lists — the Python
  runtime (PSF-2.0), OpenSSL (Apache-2.0), libffi, zlib, Qt plugins, ICU and others. List
  what the finished bundle contains and extend `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES` and `LICENSES/`.
- **Smaller inventory:** exclude Qt modules and plugins Hermes does not use (e.g. QtWebEngine,
  QtMultimedia, QML). That is not required by the licenses, but each excluded module is one
  license fewer to check and makes the bundle smaller.
- **Frida gadgets:** they are downloaded at runtime and not part of the bundle. If a bundle
  ever ships them, their wxWindows licence text must be in it as well (`LICENSES/Frida.txt`).

```

`SECURITY.md`:

```md
# Security Policy

## Supported versions

Hermes Hook is in early alpha. Only the latest release and the current `main` branch receive fixes.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please do **not** open a public issue for security problems. Report them privately through GitHub instead:

1. Open the [Security tab](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/security) of the repository.
2. Click **Report a vulnerability** and describe the problem, the affected version and, if possible, the steps to reproduce it.

Hermes Hook is maintained in spare time, so answers are on a best-effort basis. You can usually expect a first reply within two weeks. Once a fix is released, the report is published as a security advisory, with credit if you want it.

## Scope

Hermes Hook attaches to processes, injects code into them and runs JavaScript from hooks, templates and scripts. Some of this is intended behaviour, not a vulnerability. Reports are welcome for, for example:

- code from Hermes running somewhere it should not, e.g. an imported file that executes code without the user running it on purpose;
- Hermes weakening the security of the system beyond what attaching to a process needs, e.g. files or sockets other users can access;
- leaks of personal data, e.g. into exported files or bug reports.

Out of scope:

- Hook templates, scripts and exports from other people run code in the game by design. Only import files from sources you trust.
- Anti-cheat or anti-tamper systems detecting Hermes, and bans that result from it. Hermes is meant for single-player games only (see the [README](README.md#disclaimer)).
- Crashes or changed behaviour of the game you attached Hermes to. Please report those as a normal [bug](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/issues/new/choose).

```

`docs/development/architecture.md`:

```md
# Architecture

Hermes is a PySide6 application in one Python package, `hermes`. The code that runs inside the game is JavaScript for [Frida](https://frida.re), kept in `.js` files beside the Python module that loads it.

## Packages

The packages form layers; each depends only on the layers below it.

```mermaid
flowchart BT
    agent["agent<br/><small>base of every Frida agent</small>"]
    platform["platform<br/><small>OS differences, host side</small>"]
    core["core<br/><small>memory, scans, pointers, settings, logs</small>"]
    attach["attach<br/><small>Frida sessions, Wine gadget, ptrace</small>"]
    engines["engines<br/><small>Mono, IL2CPP, Unreal adapters</small>"]
    hooks["hooks<br/><small>hook engine, templates</small>"]
    features["features<br/><small>watch, trace, monitor, scripts, …</small>"]
    db["db<br/><small>SQLAlchemy models, repositories</small>"]
    ui["ui<br/><small>main window, widgets, themes</small>"]
    platform --> core
    core --> attach
    agent --> engines
    platform --> engines
    attach --> hooks
    engines --> hooks
    hooks --> features
    features --> db
    db --> ui
```

| Package | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `hermes/agent` | What every agent builds on: loading agent sources (`source.py`), errors in the user's language (`messages.js`), what differs between Linux and Windows inside the game (`platform.js`). Imports nothing else from Hermes. |
| `hermes/platform` | Hermes' own side of a process: reading memory and mappings, process facts (`linux.py`, `windows.py`), PE images of Wine processes (`wine.py`). |
| `hermes/core` | Memory access, the value scanner, pointer chains and value types; settings, logs, the activity log and the session registry. |
| `hermes/attach` | Getting into a process: Frida sessions (`frida_attach.py`), the Wine gadget and its Windows helper (`wine_gadget.py`, `wine_helper.py`, `inject/`), shared ptrace machinery (`ptrace_engine.py`), the watch backend names. |
| `hermes/engines` | One adapter per engine (`mono/`, `il2cpp/`, `unreal/`), each with a Python adapter and its agent; `registry.py` combines them into the engine agent the features load. |
| `hermes/hooks` | The hook engine (`engine.py` + `engine.js`), the ptrace hook, the built-in manipulations and templates (`transforms.py`), the script sandbox. |
| `hermes/features` | The tools: write watch, freeze, catalog, trace, native trace, monitors, method hooks and calls, scripts, favorites, call graph. |
| `hermes/db` | SQLite through SQLAlchemy: models and repositories, export and import. |
| `hermes/ui` | The main window, widgets, localization, themes, icons. |

## Agents

A feature's agent is put together from parts: the platform helpers (`agent/platform.js` with `agent/messages.js`), the engine prelude, every engine adapter's agent, the engine facade, and the feature's own script. The engine adapters register themselves; the facade picks the one whose runtime the game has loaded, so features use one `engine` object whatever the engine.

Under Wine/Proton the agents run in Frida's Windows gadget. The gadget drops messages larger than 128 KiB, so `attach/frida_attach.py` sends larger agents in parts.

## Built-in hook templates

The example templates (Multiplier, Fixed value, Clamp and the method templates) come from subclasses of `ValueTransform` in `hermes/hooks/transforms.py` whose `kind` is in `EXAMPLE_TEMPLATE_KINDS`. If an example is missing at start (same seed key or name), Hermes creates it. Name, description and parameter labels come from `EXAMPLE_TEXTS` in the same file, under `<kind>`, `<kind>.description`, `<kind>.<parameter>` and `choice.<value>`; where they are missing, `title`, the parameter name or the choice value is used. Examples created by earlier versions with German names are renamed through `GERMAN_EXAMPLE_TEXTS`. Manipulations of your own do not need this: they are created as templates directly in the interface.

## Adding an engine

1. Add a subpackage under `hermes/engines/` with an `EngineAdapter` subclass (see `engines/base.py`) and an `agent.js` that registers itself with `registerEngine(...)`.
2. List the adapter in `ENGINES` in `engines/registry.py`; the order is the order in which the agent looks for runtimes.
3. Declare its capabilities; the UI enables the tools the adapter supports.

The [roadmap](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/blob/main/ROADMAP.md) discusses candidates such as Godot, Lua engines, RPG Maker and Ren'Py.

```

`docs/development/implementation-notes.md`:

```md
# Implementation notes

What was learned while building the features: how they work inside, what broke in which game, and why the code does what it does. Open work is in the [roadmap](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).

## Native call diff trace

The engine-independent native counterpart of the Mono trace. Frida's **Stalker** records which
functions or basic blocks a thread executes. Comparing a baseline with a scenario finds the
functions called newly or more often when, for example, paying or taking damage.

- Model: Cheat Engine's "Code Filter" / "Ultimap"
- Verified with the test game under Proton and Baldur's Gate under Proton; see the findings below.

**Implementation (2026-10-19 onward):** View → "Native trace…", independent of any engine.
`hermes/features/native_trace.py` (`NativeTraceWorker`) and `native_trace.js` (agent),
`hermes/ui/widgets/native_trace.py` (window). Session logic shared with the Mono trace in
`AgentWorker` (`hermes/features/trace.py`); `analyze` and the verdicts are the same.

- Stalker follows the chosen threads with a CModule `transform` (since 2026-10-22, before
  that `events: {call: true}` and `onCallSummary`): before every `call` of the followed code
  sits a callout in C that works out the target from the registers (direct, register, memory
  operand including `rip`-relative) and counts it in a hash table, in the game's thread. The
  order of the first calls is exact and knows the call site. x86/x64 only; a `call` through
  `fs:`/`gs:` is not counted. Modules not chosen run natively through `Stalker.exclude` (only
  calls *into* them count). Preselection: the modules in the game's folder, the threads
  running right now (CPU time or context switches in `/proc`). Under Wine (2026-10-29) the
  game's folder comes from `GetModuleHandleW(NULL)`: Frida's `Process.mainModule` is just
  the first module listed there (`netapi32.dll` in Dark Souls III), which preselected the
  system DLLs and not the game. The agent measures the threads itself with
  `GetThreadTimes`, since /proc does not know Windows thread ids; before, every thread was
  preselected. Dark Souls III: 5 game modules, 20 of 86 threads.
- Function names: exports, on Linux also symbols (`DebugSymbol`), otherwise `module+0x…`.
- Verified: test game (C) and a Python interpreter with `libpython` (~6 million calls/2 s,
  the scenario found the JSON encoder), and Baldur's Gate under Proton (see below).
- Learned: Stalker's queue holds 16 384 events per drain by default and drops the rest
  **silently**. With the CModule there is no queue any more; calls are only lost when the
  function table (2^19) is full (`lost`, warned about in the window).
- Learned (2026-10-22): on x86-64 every new 4 MB code slab of Stalker must lie within ±2 GB
  of its thread context, which Gum maps without a hint. EVERSPACE (UE4, 9.9 GB in 5700
  regions) left no such room there: `gum_memory_allocate_near` returned NULL, Stalker wrote
  to `0x18` and the game crashed 0.4 s after the start (Pillars of Eternity after 20–40 s,
  same cause). The agent now fills every gap above the highest free area of 256 MB with
  placeholders while Stalker creates the contexts (`withRoomNearby`, Linux x86-64), so they
  land at the top of that area. EVERSPACE: 34 threads followed, baseline recorded, clean
  stop. Test: `test_native_trace_survives_a_crowded_address_space` (crashes without it).
- Learned: Frida's TinyCC has no compare-and-swap (`g_atomic_*_compare_and_exchange`,
  `__atomic_*`, `__sync_*` are missing), only `g_atomic_int_add`: entries are taken through a
  claim counter. Load test with libpython (4 threads): ~11 million calls/2 s without loss,
  the scenario slightly faster than with `onCallSummary` (1.2 s instead of 1.5 s).
- Learned (2026-10-22): under Windows, `Stalker.follow(id)` takes another thread over through
  a hardware breakpoint at the instruction it stands at, nearly always the return of a system
  call in `ntdll`. Wine keeps the breakpoint after Stalker cleared it in the exception's
  context. Stalker's handler itself calls `Sleep` while taking the thread over, through the
  same return: the breakpoint hit again inside the handler, which then waited for a lock it
  already held. The game froze (winedbg: all game threads in Frida's handler, waiting on an
  SRW lock), or it crashed later with `EXCEPTION_SINGLE_STEP`. This affected the old agent
  too (test game under Proton: 3 of 5 runs froze). Removing the breakpoint from the agent
  thread is a race; `NtSetContextThread` on the thread itself from a vectored exception
  handler placed first has no effect under Wine. Now each thread follows itself (no
  breakpoint): `Thread.backtrace(…, FUZZY)` finds its next return address into a followed
  module, and a one-shot Interceptor hook there calls `Stalker.follow()` in the thread. Test
  game under Proton: 10 of 10 runs clean, and only this way is the render thread really
  followed (8379 instead of 585 calls). Threads without a return into followed code count as
  not followable; those that have not entered yet are in `waiting`. Remaining risk: the hook
  overwrites a few bytes after a `call` instruction; if code jumps into the middle of them,
  the game crashes.
- Reproducing without a game: a small Windows test game built with `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc`,
  run with Proton's `files/bin/wine` in a `WINEPREFIX` of its own; Hermes connects through
  the gadget as with a real game. Stacks in the frozen state: `wine winedbg --command
  "bt all" <Windows PID>` (gdb only sees Wine's Unix side).
- Learned: a followed thread that hangs in a blocking call holds on to Stalker's code;
  `script.unload()` then waits up to ~25 s (the game survives). So idle threads are not
  preselected, and "Stop following" does not unload the agent at once. A new trace gets a
  fresh agent, because Stalker cannot take exclusions back.
- Learned (2026-10-29): Baldur's Gate under Proton froze on the second "Stop following"
  (two agents, so two Stalkers in the process): the followed main thread looped in Frida's
  own code, calling `NtSetContextThread` with a broken context (a write to `0x2d9`), and
  Proton's log grew by about 40 MB/s with the access violations. Under Windows the threads
  now stop following themselves, as they start: `stop` sets a flag, and the C callout
  calls `leave()` (`Stalker.unfollow()` of its own thread) at the thread's next call;
  threads that do not run meanwhile stay followed and are reported (`staying`), never
  taken over from outside. One agent serves every trace; a fresh one is loaded only when
  a module to follow was excluded before. Checked with a Windows test game under Proton
  (stop, second trace, dispose); the freeze itself did not occur there with the old code
  either, so the cause is not proven. Setting the trace's flag needs no exclusions to
  change: Stalker's exclusions must not change while threads are followed (a module
  observer doing so crashed Baldur's Gate and Dark Souls III).

- **(2026-10-22):** freezing under Wine/Proton fixed, see above. Confirmed with Baldur's
  Gate under Proton Experimental (1 thread, `Baldur.exe`: 3.2 million calls in the baseline,
  nothing lost, ended cleanly). The 32-bit path of the native trace under Wine is untested
  (Shadowrun Returns is Mono, where native tools ask first: they crashed it); the gadget itself runs in
  32-bit games (Mono trace in Shadowrun Returns).

- **(2026-10-19):** results sortable and filterable (name, call count, `%3`). Native
  function monitor (`hermes/features/native_monitor.py`): an Interceptor on a function from
  the trace or by address/module+offset/symbol; logs arguments, result and caller, and
  compares the memory behind pointer arguments before and after the call (for C++ methods:
  which fields of `this` are set). Not yet tried in Baldur's Gate (native, Linux).

## IL2CPP adapter

**IL2CPP adapter (2026-11-03):** `hermes/engines/il2cpp/` (`Il2CppAdapter`, agent in
`agent.js`), tried on V Rising (Unity 2022.3, metadata v31, Proton). Recognised by
`GameAssembly.dll`/`.so`; the runtime counts as started once `il2cpp_get_corlib` answers.
- Catalog: images without `.dll` as assembly names, signatures as Mono writes them, the
  PE time stamp and size of GameAssembly as MVID. 139 assemblies, 43,000 classes in V Rising.
- Naming: a table of all method code starts (230,000 methods, under a second), built on the
  agent's thread after attaching. The function holding an address comes from the unwind data
  (`RtlLookupFunctionEntry` on Windows, `.eh_frame_hdr` on Linux); it belongs to a method only
  if it starts at one. Abstract methods are left out, their pointer is a shared stub.
- Trace: `compileAll` hands out the code pointers; nothing to compile or undo.
- Shared code: about a quarter of the methods share their code with others (folded identical
  functions, shared generics; one empty constructor stands for 8,400 methods in V Rising).
- Probed for the next steps: Unity calls `il2cpp_runtime_invoke` on the main thread about
  17,000 times a second (also on job threads, to be filtered out), so the Mono way of running
  work on the main thread carries over to calls. Arguments: IL2CPP passes a hidden
  `MethodInfo*` last. The call graph would need disassembly instead of IL.
- Method monitor (2026-11-03): signatures, fields and properties as Mono gives them; the
  monitor reads a struct result's hidden pointer before `this` (`returnPointerFirst`). Static
  data: `Il2CppClass` has no getter for it; its `klass` field points at the class itself, the
  fields array follows and `static_fields` seven pointers later (Unity 2018 and later), found
  without running a static constructor. Unity names and getters run on the main thread through
  the `il2cpp_runtime_invoke` hook. Tried in V Rising: `EventSystem "EventSystem(Clone)"`,
  properties of a MonoBehaviour and of an ECS system.
- Method hooks (2026-11-03): write barrier (`il2cpp_gc_wbarrier_set_field`), `il2cpp_string_new`,
  classes by name (`il2cpp_class_from_name`), `ctx.find` through
  `FindObjectsOfType(Type)`, which code stripping removed in V Rising: there
  `FindObjectsOfType(Type, bool)` is used. Struct methods: `this` and `il2cpp_runtime_invoke`
  both take a pointer to the struct's data (tried with `Vector3.get_magnitude`), so struct
  getters work as with Mono; the monitor shows such a `this` as the struct. Tried in V Rising
  with a read-only script on `EventSystem:Update`.
- ECS games: of 538 `OnUpdate` methods in V Rising's gameplay systems, 8 ran as IL2CPP code;
  the rest are Burst-compiled. Their data lies in ECS chunks, not in objects.

## Unreal adapter

**Unreal adapter (2026-10-30):** `hermes/engines/unreal/` (`UnrealAdapter`, agent in
`agent.js`). Recognised by the executable's name (`<Project>-Win64-Shipping.exe`, also Linux
and modular builds). The agent finds `FNamePool` and `GUObjectArray` in the module's
writable data by their shape (pool: `CurrentBlock`, `Blocks[]`, first entries `None` and
`ByteProperty`; objects: `MaxElements`/`NumElements` matching `MaxChunks`/`NumChunks`), then
measures the offsets of UStruct, FField/FProperty and UFunction on objects every game has
(CoreUObject's `Class`, `Object`, `Vector`, `Transform`, `Object:ExecuteUbergraph`).

- Verified in **Avowed** (UE5, Proton Experimental): found in 0.8 s, 260 000 objects read in
  0.4 s. Catalog: 168 package groups, `/Script/Alabama` with 1573 classes and 4831 UFunctions.
  Trace over `/Script/Alabama` + `/Game/Blueprints`: 4935 hooks in 0.65 s, baseline and
  scenario recorded, Blueprint functions restored on stop, game stayed up.
- Learned: Avowed's `FUObjectItem` is 0x14 bytes (packed), not 0x18; FField's owner is a
  tagged 8-byte pointer (Next at 0x18, name at 0x20), older UE5 has 16 bytes there. Hence
  item size and offsets are measured, not assumed.
- Learned: on Linux most of `.bss` is an anonymous mapping right after the module, which
  Frida's `Module.enumerateRanges` leaves out; the agent adds the ranges that follow the
  module's own.
- Learned: the trace's selection (`[[assembly, token], ...]`) passed 128 KiB for 5000
  methods and cut the gadget's connection under Wine; it now goes to the agent in parts
  (`choose`) before `start`. That affected large Mono traces under Wine as well.
- Catalog tokens are a hash of package, class and function name (object indexes change
  between runs); the catalog cache's build id is a hash of the declared functions.
- Trace: native UFunctions are hooked at their exec thunk (`Func`); every Blueprint function
  shares the interpreter (`ProcessInternal`) as `Func`, so each gets a stub of its own
  (16 nops, `jmp [rip]`, allocated with `allocateCode`, never freed) as `Func`, which
  `releaseCode` undoes after the trace. Calls the trace cannot see: C++ calling C++, and
  Blueprint code calling a Blueprint function directly (`CallFunction` runs the script
  without `Func`).

- **(2026-10-30):** method monitor and object inspector. `prepare` answers
  `frame: true`; `callFrame` reads the `FFrame` (Node 0x10, Object 0x18, Code 0x20, Locals
  0x28, checked in Avowed): through ProcessEvent `Node` is the function and `Locals` its
  parameters; from Blueprint bytecode `Code` points at the argument expressions, of which
  local and instance variables, constants and `self` are decoded. The result is read from
  the frame's `Result` pointer. Avowed: player, companions, encounters (`AActor*`, enums,
  floats) decoded live. Learned: for interface functions `Context` points into the object
  (the interface part, e.g. +0x318); `Stack.Object` is the object, from bytecode the agent
  searches back for the object table's entry.
- **(2026-10-30):** callers in the monitor. From bytecode the frame passed is the
  caller's (`Node` + `Code` = `Class:Function+0x…` in its bytecode); through ProcessEvent the
  agent scans up to 256 KiB of the thread's stack for FFrame's vtable (learned from the
  first frame it sees) and takes the nearest frame whose Node is a UFunction, Object alive
  and Code inside Node's bytecode. Avowed: `MinimapIconInterface:DetermineMinimapIconType`
  ← `WBP_InGameHUDWindow_C:Tick+0x35`. Without a script frame above, the native return
  address stays. The trace's callers could use the same.
- **(2026-10-30):** method hooks for UFunctions (change arguments in `Locals`, the
  result at `Result`).
- **(2026-10-30):** calling UFunctions and scripts. `UObject::ProcessEvent` is the one
  virtual function of `Default__Object`'s vtable whose code calls `[reg + Func]` (Avowed:
  slot 77); calls run on the game thread (the main thread: Avowed 348), queued until it
  next enters ProcessEvent, where a temporary interceptor runs them. The parameter block
  is laid out from the function's properties; FStrings point at buffers of the agent (the
  game copies them), FNames are looked up among the objects' names, static functions run
  on the class default object. Avowed: `BP_CheatManager_C` (an `AlabamaCheatManager`) is
  the player controller's `CheatManager` (+0x400); 147 of its 152 functions have code in
  the shipping build (`GiveHealth`, `AddCurrency`, `ToggleUnlimitedStamina` checked live).
  Scripts (hermes/features/scripts.py) run such calls by time. Hooks on functions a call
  reaches do not fire for it (Frida's interceptor ignores the thread inside a callback).
- **(2026-10-31):** scripts in the game export.
- **(2026-10-31):** Unreal in the **Call method** dialog. FString and FName as text, bools
  as a checkbox, enums by name; a struct whose fields are all numbers (FVector) is typed field
  by field (`1 2 3` or `X=1; Z=3`), its bytes built in Python from the fields `describe_call`
  adds (Mono's structs of numbers get them too). Outputs (`CPF_OutParm` without
  `CPF_ReferenceParm`, Blueprint's rule) need no input and are read from the parameter block
  after the call. An instance UFunction of the catalog or the favorites runs on a live object
  of its class (`call_found`, capability `CALL_FOUND`): the first one `findObject` gives, or one
  named or at an address (checked against the class). Not typed in: TArray, TMap, TSet,
  FText, delegates, structs of structs.
- **(2026-10-31):** GAS attributes window (View → "GAS attributes …"): the player's
  attribute sets, base values set through the game's own setter, held by a script. Setter
  discovery supports the standard AbilitySystemComponent/FGameplayAttribute pattern and
  AngelscriptGAS's `TrySetAttributeBaseValue(FName, float)` pattern (Gothic 1 Remake).

## Write hooks under anti-tamper protection

Found with Dark Souls III (Arxan/GuardIT):

- **Patched sites are repaired:** Arxan restores the original code of checked functions, the
  hook then stops without an error. The agent compares every site with the bytes it wrote once
  a second and reports `site-state` (hook status "Removed by game"); with the setting
  `hook_repatch` it patches a site whose original code is back again. Arxan also decrypts and
  encrypts code at run time: a site may read as "changed" for a while, and int3 padding used as
  a short jump cave can be overwritten (the cave is then looked for anew).
- **Debug registers are detected:** with debug registers set on all threads at an address that
  is never executed, the game crashed about 11 s later, jumping to the same unmapped address
  (`0x7ff7ab63b120`) as in the two crashes before (a breakpoint hook and a write watch). So
  hook installation as hardware breakpoint (`HookSpec.breakpoint`, leaves the code untouched)
  is no option there, and write watches must stay short. When a game ends within 30 s after
  Hermes used debug registers in it, the main window says so.
- **Performance:** a hooked write cost ~18 µs in a test process, mostly JavaScript work: all
  16 registers read into an object (~7 µs) and the address computed with BigInt (~3.5 µs).
  Now registers are read on demand, the address with NativePointer arithmetic from a plan made
  once per site, and caller signatures took the stack slots of the last scan first
  (`siteSignature`, since replaced by the C scan below): ~8 µs, caller check +1.5 µs instead of +3.5 µs. The rest is the transform
  and its context (~3 µs), the two calls into JS with the saved state (~1.5 µs) and reading
  the old value.
- **Frame drops came from the agent's lock, not the average cost:** measured in Dark Souls III
  (setting "Hooks: measure their cost"): 100–350 writes/s per site, most of them skipped
  (other callers), but again and again a hooked thread waited ~28–37 ms (twice a Windows
  scheduler slice), once up to 400 ms: a game thread descheduled while it held the agent's
  JavaScript lock stalls every other hooked thread.
- **C fast path (2026-10-27):** the trampoline calls a CModule (`FAST_SOURCE` in
  `hermes/hooks/engine.js`). It checks address, switch and learned callers and runs multiply, freeze and
  clamp itself (`native_spec` in `transforms.py` recognises them by their code, also copies
  such as "Clamp (Import)"). Writes pending between before and after are kept per thread in a
  table per site. A hooked write now costs ~0.1 µs instead of ~8–18 µs in the test process; a
  foreign caller is rejected in C after its first write (3003 of 3004 writes without JS).
- Learned (DS3, first try of the fast path): caching one stack layout per site (the slots of
  the last scan) did not work there: the scan finds the return address at different distances
  from rsp (stale return addresses in the locals of a large frame), the layout changed on nearly
  every write and the TP hook still ran in JavaScript. Now C runs its own copy of the scan
  (`native_frames`): slot by slot, executable values only, with a table of what the JavaScript
  scan decided about each (value, function) pair (`fast_teach_verdict`, `fast_teach_skip`).
  `GetCurrentThreadStackLimits` keeps it on the thread's stack; without it (Linux) callers are
  checked in JavaScript. Caller check ~0.1 µs; in the test a caller whose return address lay
  deeper (through `qsort`) needed JavaScript once in 56 032 writes. Dark Souls III: steady frame
  time, "0 in JS" for TP and FP. A fixed-address hook that learns callers still runs in
  JavaScript.
- Learned: the rare writes that still need JavaScript (new stack values, e.g. at a bonfire)
  took 60–120 ms each in Dark Souls III and dropped a frame: `Process.findRangeByAddress` costs
  11 ms there (it walks all ranges of the process) and the scan asked it for every stack value.
  Now both scans use one sorted snapshot of executable memory (`isExecutable`, refreshed every
  5 s, ~25 ms).

## Activity log

`hermes/core/activity.py`, `hermes/ui/activity_recorder.py`: `activity.jsonl` beside
`hermes.log`, one JSON line per event with a run id. Agents, RPCs, script errors and the end
of a session are recorded by proxies around Frida's session and script in `attach_session`
(all Frida workers go through it); sessions by `sessions.tracked`, the gadget by
`wine_gadget.connect`, process/engine/backend by the main window, clicks by a timer that
connects new controls every 500 ms (not an event filter: for a Python filter PyQt wraps the
receiver of every event, also widgets being destroyed, and crashed in sip doing so).
Snapshots of the game's threads (`/proc/<pid>/task/*`: state, CPU, system call) 1 s after a
native trace starts, at `stop` and when a session is cut; the results of every trace phase
in numbers. From three calls of the same method within 2 s, RPCs are summed up. It can be
switched off in the settings.

- Learned: an agent whose `unload` waits for a thread blocked in Stalker's code shows up as
  `agent_unloaded … seconds=25`.

## Settings

`hermes/core/settings.py` (definitions, values in this process), table `settings` in
`hermes.db` (`hermes/db/repository/settings.py`), window `hermes/ui/widgets/settings_dialog.py`
under Settings → General …: activity log, the trace's method limit under Wine/Proton
(`wine_trace_limit`, formerly the constant `WINE_TRACE_LIMIT`), from how many methods the trace
asks first (`large_trace`), entries in the traces' call sequence (`trace_sequence`), the refresh
interval of tracked addresses, automatic Wine/Proton gadget downloads (off by default), the
language, and since 2026-10-26/27 the hook options `hook_short_jump`, `hook_repatch` and
`hook_profiling` (see above). The watch backend stays in the menu and in `QSettings`, since it is
chosen automatically on attach.

## Wine and Proton

- **Method monitor and method hooks under Wine:** `hermes/features/monitor.py` now assigns
  arguments by the platform's convention: System V (Linux x86-64), Win64 (rcx, rdx, r8, r9 or
  xmm0–3 by position, 32 bytes of shadow space) and x86 (everything on the stack). Under
  32 bit, float results are in st0 and 64-bit results in edx:eax; they are read or reported
  as not readable, but not replaced.
- **32-bit Wine games:** the Windows helper also loads the x86 gadget into 32-bit games. The
  agents assumed 64 bit in three places: the batch structure of the Mono agent (Shadowrun
  Returns crashed in the COM interop check), `MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION` in `watchUnmaps`, and
  `CONTEXT` in `pauseThreads`. That is fixed and checked in a 32-bit process. The hook
  engine only handles x64 code (`installSite`), so the watch and hooks take ptrace for 32-bit
  games; Mono features always go through the gadget.
- **Gadget through the Windows helper:** `hermes/attach/inject/inject.c`, built
  with `build.sh` (MinGW or zig) as `hermes-inject-x86_64.exe` or `-x86.exe` into
  `build/inject/` (not in git; `helper_path` runs `build.sh` once if they are missing), loads the gadget
  with `VirtualAllocEx`/`WriteProcessMemory`/`CreateRemoteThread` + `LoadLibraryW`.
  `hermes/attach/wine_helper.py` starts it with the game's `wine` (beside or above its
  preloader) and its `WINEPREFIX` and sync variables. It finds the Windows PID by exe name and
  creation time. Beforehand it checks that the prefix's wineserver socket exists in `/tmp`, so
  that no second server starts. `load_gadget` tries the helper first and falls back to the
  ptrace loader for 64 bit.
  - The gadget drops messages from Hermes larger than 128 KiB; larger agents are sent in
    parts and put together in the game (`frida_attach.py`, 2026-10-27).
  - Checked in a prefix of its own with Proton's Wine (64- and 32-bit `ping.exe`, several
    processes of the same name).
- **Test-suite core dumps (2026-10-29):** a window released a worker in its
  `finished` signal, which Qt emits before the thread has ended; destroying a running QThread
  aborted the process. Workers are now kept until their thread has ended
  (`hermes/ui/workers.py`).

# Development

```bash

Many tests compile a small C program and attach to it with Frida: hooks, the watch, the native trace and monitor, the Mono features against a stand-in Mono runtime, the IL2CPP features against a stand-in `GameAssembly.so`, the Unreal features against a stand-in Unreal game. They are skipped if `gcc` is missing, `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` is not `0` or the machine is not x86-64. Tests of the Windows helper need MinGW, some need Linux.

It can also be started by hand under *Actions → docs → Run workflow*. GitHub Pages must be set to *Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions*.

# Screenshots

The screenshots in this documentation are rendered by a script, so they can be renewed after every change to the interface:

./.venv/bin/python scripts/screenshots/run.py                  # every scene, dark and light

```markdown
<figure markdown="span">

## How the scenes work

No scene attaches to a game. Each fills Hermes' widgets with demo data, the way its workers would after talking to the game, so the images are reproducible and need no game installed. Before Hermes is imported, the script points every folder Hermes writes to – Qt settings, the database, logs, caches – into a temporary directory; your own data is never touched.

The scenes live in `scripts/screenshots/scenes_*.py`; `studio.py` holds what they share. A scene is a function that returns the widget to capture:

```python
from studio import scene, settle

@scene("memory-viewer", size=(1000, 600), description="Memory around the gold")
def memory_viewer(studio):
    window = studio.show_attached()   # demo program in toolbar and status bar
    ...                               # build the widget and fill it with demo data
    return widget
```

The demo data follows the test game of the [tutorial](../getting-started/first-hook.md): `dummy_game.exe`, the gold at `0x56153A2C41F8` behind `dummy_game.exe+0x4040 → 0x28 → 0x0`.

## Screenshots of real games

Some images need a real game: the game window itself, or the effect of a change in it. They are taken by hand, as `-dark`/`-light` pairs where Hermes is in the picture, and kept in `docs/assets/photos/` as WebP (quality 88; the PNG originals there are ignored by git and the site). The pages mark the places with a box like this:

!!! screenshot "Screenshot to add: example"
    What the image should show.
    File: `docs/assets/photos/example.png`

Replace the box with the image once it exists. `grep -rn '!!! screenshot' docs/` lists the open places.

`docs/engines/index.md`:

```md
# Engines

Memory scans, the write watch, hooks and the native tools work with any game. For games built on **Unity** (Mono or IL2CPP) and **Unreal Engine**, Hermes also reads the engine's own metadata: the classes and methods of the game, the fields of its objects. That opens a second way in: instead of searching for a value and the instruction that writes it, you find the method that does the work and change its arguments or result.

Hermes recognises the engine when it attaches; the status bar names it.

## What each engine offers

| Tool | Unity (Mono) | Unity (IL2CPP) | Unreal Engine |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| [Catalog](#catalog) of classes and methods | :material-check: | :material-check: | :material-check: |
| [Assemblies / packages](#assemblies) | :material-check: | :material-check: | :material-check: |
| [Trace](#trace) | :material-check: | :material-check: | :material-check: |
| [Method monitor](#method-monitor) | :material-check: | :material-check: | :material-check: |
| [Object inspector](#object-inspector) | :material-check: | :material-check: | :material-check: |
| [Method hooks](#method-hooks) | :material-check: | :material-check: | :material-check: |
| [Call method](#call-method) | :material-check: | – | :material-check: |
| [Call graph](#call-graph) | :material-check: | – | – |
| [Scripts](../guide/scripts.md) | :material-check: | :material-check: | :material-check: |
| [GAS attributes](unreal.md#gas-attributes) | – | – | :material-check: |

The engine pages describe the details: [Unity (Mono)](unity-mono.md), [Unity (IL2CPP)](unity-il2cpp.md), [Unreal Engine](unreal.md).

## Catalog

**View → Catalog …** lists the game's classes and methods, grouped by assembly (Unity) or package (Unreal), with a filter. Methods carry their signature, e.g. `Ns.Class:Method (int,single)`. From a method the context menu leads to the monitor, a method hook, the call dialog, the call graph or a favorite (★).

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Catalog](../assets/screenshots/catalog-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Catalog](../assets/screenshots/catalog-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

A catalog read once is cached; **View → Catalog (offline) …** opens it without the game running.

## Assemblies

**View → Assemblies …** limits the catalog and the trace to chosen assemblies (Unreal: packages). The choice is saved per program. Without a choice both use all of the game's assemblies, and leave out those of the engine and the framework.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Assemblies](../assets/screenshots/assemblies-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="560" }
  ![Assemblies](../assets/screenshots/assemblies-light.webp#only-light){ width="560" }
</figure>

## Trace

**View → Trace …** finds the methods that a scenario in the game calls – *which method runs when I buy something?* It hooks the methods of the chosen assemblies and works like the [native trace](../guide/native-tools.md): a **baseline** while the game idles, then the **scenario**; the methods that are new or called more often in the scenario are the candidates. Preselection filters keep large games manageable.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Trace](../assets/screenshots/trace-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Trace](../assets/screenshots/trace-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

## Method monitor

The method monitor logs the calls of chosen methods with their arguments, the result and the object they run on.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Method monitor](../assets/screenshots/method-monitor-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Method monitor](../assets/screenshots/method-monitor-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

## Object inspector

The object inspector shows the fields of an object – for Unity also static fields and properties, for Unreal the UProperties of objects and structs – evaluated on the game's main thread. Open it from an object in the monitor or a script result; fields that hold a value can be handed to the tracked addresses.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Object inspector](../assets/screenshots/object-inspector-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Object inspector](../assets/screenshots/object-inspector-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

## Method hooks

A method hook changes a method's arguments or the fields of its object before it runs, or its result after it. Like value hooks, method hooks use [templates](../guide/templates.md) – their script sees the method's arguments and `ctx.this` – and they are stored per program and reinstalled at the next start.

Method hook scripts can reach other game code: `ctx.call` calls a static method, `ctx.static` reads static fields, `ctx.find("ClassName")` gives a live object of a class.

## Call method

**Call method** runs a method of the game on its main thread with arguments you enter, and shows the result. See the engine pages for what each engine supports.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Call method](../assets/screenshots/method-call-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Call method](../assets/screenshots/method-call-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
</figure>

## Call graph

For Mono games the call graph shows which methods a method calls and which call it, read from the IL code.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Call graph](../assets/screenshots/call-graph-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Call graph](../assets/screenshots/call-graph-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

`docs/engines/unity-il2cpp.md`:

```md
# Unity (IL2CPP)

Unity games built with IL2CPP translate their C# code to C++ ahead of time; there is no Mono runtime and no IL in the game. Hermes reads such games through the `il2cpp_*` API that `GameAssembly.dll` (or `GameAssembly.so`) exports.

- The **catalog**, **Assemblies …** and the **trace** work as for Mono, with the same signatures (`Ns.Class:Method (int,single)`).
- Code addresses in `GameAssembly` are named as the C# method they belong to: in the trace's callers, in the [write watch](../guide/write-watch.md) and at hook sites. IL2CPP keeps no table from code to methods, so Hermes builds one when it attaches; function bounds come from the module's unwind data.
- The **method monitor** logs calls with arguments, results and the object they run on (with its Unity name, or the struct for a struct's methods); the **object inspector** shows fields, static fields and properties, evaluated on the game's main thread.
- **Method hooks** work as for Mono: scripts change arguments, fields and results and use `ctx.call`, `ctx.static` and `ctx.find`.

## Shared code

Many methods share one piece of code: the linker folds identical functions, and generic code is shared. Their names end in `[shared with N]`, and the trace counts them under the first. A hook on such code affects every method sharing it.

## Not yet available

- The **Call method** dialog and the **call graph** (IL2CPP keeps no IL).
- Games built on Unity's ECS run much of their logic as Burst code, which method hooks do not see. In V Rising most gameplay systems are Burst-compiled; their data lies in ECS chunks rather than objects.

## Tested games

V Rising (Unity 2022.3, metadata v31, Proton).

```

`docs/engines/unity-mono.md`:

```md
# Unity (Mono)

Unity games built with Mono ship their code as .NET assemblies (`Assembly-CSharp.dll` and others) and compile it at run time. Hermes talks to the Mono runtime in the game – `libmono`/`mono-2.0-bdwgc.dll` – through its exported API, natively on Linux and under Wine/Proton on Windows games.

Everything in the [engine overview](index.md) is available:

- The **catalog** lists the classes and methods of the game's assemblies, also offline for games read before.
- **Assemblies …** limits the catalog and the trace to chosen assemblies.
- The **trace** finds the methods a scenario calls, with preselection filters. Mono compiles every traced method first, which takes a moment for large selections; from a configurable number of methods Hermes asks before it starts.
- The **method monitor** logs calls with arguments and results; **method hooks** change arguments, fields or results with templates of their own.
- The **call graph** shows which methods a method calls and which call it, from the IL code.
- The **object inspector** shows the fields of C# objects, and **Call method** runs a static method on the game's main thread.

!!! tip "Try it on HermesQuest"
    HermesQuest is a small Unity Mono role-playing game made for trying out Hermes – the running example of the [Examples](../examples/index.md) section. Download it for [Linux](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/releases/download/v0.5.0-alpha/HermesQuest-RPG-Linux) or [Windows](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/releases/download/v0.5.0-alpha/HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip) (also for Wine/Proton); both are zip archives. The examples walk through scans, pointer scans, value and method hooks and scripts on it.

## Mono and value hooks

Code compiled by Mono lies in no module and moves with every start. Hermes therefore names a hit of the [write watch](../guide/write-watch.md) in JIT code by its C# method, and a [hook](../guide/hooks.md) with a pointer chain remembers that method: after a restart Mono compiles it and the hook is installed in it right away.

## Example: Pillars of Eternity

Pillars of Eternity (native Linux build) shows what the engine tools do in a real game.

### A cheat function from the catalog

Its assembly keeps a static class `Scripts` with the developers' console commands. Typing `scripts player` into the catalog's filter finds them, among them `GivePlayerMoney (int)`:

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Catalog in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-catalog-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Catalog in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-catalog-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The catalog filtered for <code>scripts player</code>: 8 of 30480 methods.</figcaption>
</figure>

A [script](../guide/scripts.md) with a number parameter `amount` calls it. **Copy signature** in the catalog gives the name to paste:

```js
const value = Math.trunc(ctx.args.amount);   // the method takes an int
ctx.call("Scripts:GivePlayerMoney (int)", value);
return "Gold increased by " + value;
```

`ctx.call` ignores the parameter list `(int)`; it picks the method with as many parameters as arguments given. `Math.trunc` cuts off decimals that someone may type into the number field.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Script giving money in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-script-money-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Script giving money in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-script-money-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The script's result in the log, and the game's own message: the money went through the game's code.</figcaption>
</figure>

### A method hook on the damage

Every hit in Pillars of Eternity goes through `Health:DoDamage(DamageInfo damage, GameObject attacker)`. The [method monitor](index.md#method-monitor) shows a call with its arguments: the object hit (`this`), the `DamageInfo` and the attacking GameObject. **Object details** opens each in the object inspector, where the field `m_damageBase` of `DamageInfo` turns up.

A method hook **before the call** changes that field before the game uses it. The attacker is a GameObject; `component("CharacterStats")` gives its component with the character's stats, whose `IsPartyMember` tells the party from its enemies:

```js
const stats = ctx.args.attacker && ctx.args.attacker.component("CharacterStats");
const base_old = ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase;

if (stats && !stats.IsPartyMember)
  ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase *= 0.3;   // enemies deal 30 %

if (stats && stats.IsPartyMember)
  ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase *= 20;    // the party deals 20 times the damage

ctx.log("Damagebase old/new:", base_old, "/", ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase);
```

`ctx.args.attacker && …` guards against hits without an attacker (traps, falling), where the argument is `null`.

# Unreal Engine

Hermes supports Unreal Engine 4.23 and later, 64-bit, natively and under Proton. It finds the engine's reflection data – `FNamePool` and `GUObjectArray` – in memory by its shape, without signatures, SDK dumps or a mod loader, and measures the layout of objects, properties and functions on the game itself.

- The **catalog** lists the classes and UFunctions with C++ parameter types, grouped by package: `/Script/<Module>` for C++ classes, the first folder for Blueprints (`/Game/Blueprints`).
- **Assemblies …** (here: packages) and the **trace** work as for Mono. The trace hooks the exec thunks of native UFunctions and gives every Blueprint function a hookable stub of its own. It sees calls from Blueprints and through `ProcessEvent` (events, delegates), not C++ calling C++ directly – the [native trace](../guide/native-tools.md) sees those.
- The **method monitor** logs UFunction calls with the object they run on (with its UObject name), arguments and result; the **object inspector** shows the UProperties of objects and structs. Arguments come from the parameters `ProcessEvent` passes, or, when a Blueprint calls a native function, from the bytecode of the call (variables and constants; other arguments show as `?`).
- **Method hooks** change arguments (from `ProcessEvent`'s parameters, or ref arguments from Blueprint code) and fields before a call, or the result after it. Their scripts can call UFunctions: `obj.call("Function", ...args)` runs it through `UObject::ProcessEvent` on the game thread, and `ctx.find("ClassName")` gives a live object of a class, e.g. the game's cheat manager.

## Call method

**Call method** runs a UFunction through `ProcessEvent` on the game thread: a static one on its class default object, an instance one (from the catalog or favorites) on a live object of its class – the first one found, or the one whose name or address you type in.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Call method](../assets/screenshots/method-call-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Call method](../assets/screenshots/method-call-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
  <figcaption><code>AlabamaCheatManager:GiveHealth</code> in Avowed.</figcaption>
</figure>

| Parameter type | Entered as |
| --- | --- |
| `FString`, `FName` | text |
| `bool` | checkbox |
| enums | by name |
| structs of numbers (`FVector`, …) | `1 2 3` or `X=1; Z=3` |
| outputs | nothing; shown after the call |

Not possible as arguments: `TArray`, `TMap`, `TSet`, `FText` and delegates.

Many shipping builds keep their cheat manager: in Avowed `BP_CheatManager_C` (an `AlabamaCheatManager`) has 147 functions with code, such as `GiveHealth`, `AddCurrency` and `ToggleUnlimitedStamina`.

## GAS attributes

Games built on Unreal's Gameplay Ability System keep values such as health, strength or damage multipliers as *attributes*. **View → GAS attributes …** shows the player's attribute sets with base and current value, live.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![GAS attributes](../assets/screenshots/gas-attributes-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![GAS attributes](../assets/screenshots/gas-attributes-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

GAS computes the current value anew from the base value and the active effects, so writing it into memory does not last. A base value set in the window goes through the game's own setter instead (found by its parameters; in Avowed `AlabamaAbilitySystemBlueprintLibrary:SetFloatAttributeBaseFromAbilitySystemComponent`), and the active effects keep counting: in Avowed `DamageOutgoingMult` 3 with a +40 % bonus deals 4.2 times the damage.

**Hold** keeps a value against the game resetting it (loading, levelling up) with a script in the [Scripts](../guide/scripts.md) tab. Scripts can do the same with `ctx.gas.get("Might")` and `ctx.gas.setBase("AttributeSetCore.Might", 14)`.

In Avowed, filter the window for `might` and double-click the base value: the character sheet follows at once.
