`docs/examples/hermesquest-hooks.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest: hooks

Hermes has two kinds of hooks, and HermesQuest is built to show both:

| | Value hook | Method hook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catches | one **write instruction**, found with the write watch | one **method** of the game, found in the catalog |
| Sees | the old and the new value | the method's arguments, its object (`this`) and its result |
| Works in | every game | Unity (Mono, IL2CPP) and Unreal games |
| Script | a [hook template](../guide/templates.md) | a [method script](#method-hooks) |

The examples assume you have tracked Gold, Mana and Health as in [Scans and pointer scan](hermesquest-scans.md), ideally with pointer chains.

## Value hooks

### Ten times the gold

1. Right-click "Gold" → **Address watch (writes)**.
2. Kill an enemy in the game. The watch lists one row: the instruction that added the gold. In a Mono game the code was compiled at run time and lies in no module, so Hermes names it by its C# method: `AddGold` of the class `Character`, plus an offset into it.
3. Select the row → **Create hook**, template **Multiplier**, factor `10`, **Increases only**.

From now on every kill brings ten times the gold. The column **Last** in the Hooks tab shows each write as *old → written by the game ⇒ stored*, e.g. `12 → 17 ⇒ 62`.

What happens: the game executes `Stats.Gold += amount`. The hook sits on exactly that instruction and replaces the result with `old + (new − old) × 10`. The game's own code and the log don't know about it – the log still says "5 gold", the character sheet shows the multiplied amount.

!!! tip "After a restart"
    Code compiled by Mono moves with every start. A value hook in such code remembers its C# method: when HermesQuest starts again, Hermes has Mono compile `AddGold` and installs the hook in it right away. This needs the tracked address to have a pointer chain; see [Hooks after a restart](../guide/hooks.md#after-a-restart).

### Protecting the player, not the enemies

Health shows the classic problem of **shared code**: player and enemies are both `Character`, and the same instruction in `TakeDamage` lowers everyone's health.

1. Track the player's Health (`float`, 50 at the start; take a hit, then **Decreased**).
2. Right-click it → **Address watch (writes)**, then let an enemy hit you, and rest with **R**.

The watch shows more than one row, because three methods write health:

| Method | When |
| --- | --- |
| `Character:TakeDamage` | every hit, on player and enemies |
| `Character:Heal` | resting with R |
| `Character:LevelUp` | a new level refills health |

Select the `TakeDamage` row → **Create hook**. Instead of a built-in template, use one of your own: in **View → Hook templates …** create a template "Halve damage" with this function:

```js
ctx => ctx.delta < 0 ? ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2 : ctx.new
```

Read it as: *if the value goes down (`ctx.delta < 0`), store the old value plus half the change, otherwise keep what the game wrote.* The [JavaScript page](javascript.md#arrow-functions-and-the-conditional-operator) explains each part.

Although the instruction also lowers the enemies' health, the hook only acts on **its target**: the player's Health address, resolved through the pointer chain at every write. Enemies still take full damage. The debug window shows it – select the hook, click **Debug**, and fight: the enemies' writes appear as skipped, with the reason "writes another address".

!!! warning "Why the pointer chain matters here"
    Without a pointer chain, a hook recognises its target after a restart by the *callers* that wrote it (see [caller learning](../guide/hooks.md#after-a-restart)). Here that cannot work: player and enemies are hurt through the same call chain (`ApplyDamage → TakeDamage`), so the callers are the same. Give Health a pointer chain before relying on this hook across restarts.

!!! example "Variations"
    - **Never below 1 health:** template **Clamp**, minimum `1`. The player can still be hit, but not killed.
    - **No damage at all:** template **Fixed value** on the `TakeDamage` row, with your maximum health as value. Resting and level-ups still work, because they are other instructions.

## Method hooks

A method hook does not need the write watch. It catches a whole method, and its script sees the method's arguments by name. For HermesQuest the right place for anything about damage is `Combat.CalculateDamage`: every hit of everyone goes through it, and its result is the damage that will be dealt.

### Find the method and watch it

1. **View → Catalog …**, type `CalculateDamage` into the filter.
2. Select the method `CalculateDamage` of the class `Combat` – its parameters show as `(Character,Character,single)`, `single` being C#'s name for `float` – and click **Monitor**.
3. Fight a little. The method monitor lists every call with its arguments – `attacker`, `target`, `baseDamage` – and the result.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Method monitor](../assets/screenshots/method-monitor-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Method monitor](../assets/screenshots/method-monitor-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The method monitor shows each call with its object, arguments, result and caller (here in another Mono game).</figcaption>
</figure>

Select the method in the monitor and click **Create hook …**. The dialog asks for a template and for **When** the script runs:

- **After the call: change the result** – the script sees `ctx.result` and can return a new one.
- **Before the call: change arguments and fields** – the script can change `ctx.args` and objects before the method uses them.

### Everyone hits twice as hard

Template **Result × factor**, factor `2`, after the call. Every damage, of the player and of the enemies, is doubled. The message log still shows `x1 x1` as multipliers, but the damage dealt is doubled; the F1 view marks the result as changed.

That is rarely what you want. The next step makes the hook tell attacker and target apart.

### Only the player hits harder, and takes less

Template **Method script**, after the call, with this code:

```js
// After Combat.CalculateDamage: ctx.result is the damage it computed.
if (ctx.args.attacker.IsPlayer)
  return ctx.result * 3;      // the player deals three times the damage
if (ctx.args.target.IsPlayer)
  return ctx.result / 2;      // and takes half
// no return: every other hit stays as it is
```

Line by line:

- `ctx.args.attacker` is the method's first argument, a `Character` object. `.IsPlayer` reads its field `IsPlayer` from the game's memory – `true` or `false`.
- `return ctx.result * 3` ends the script and replaces the method's result. The game then deals that damage.
- If neither condition holds, the script ends without `return`, and the game keeps its own result.

Lines starting with `//` are comments and change nothing.

### God mode, the right way: before the call

Suppose you want the player to take no damage at all. A hook *after* `Character.TakeDamage` comes too late: that method has already lowered `Stats.Health` when it returns; its result is only the health lost. So hook it **before the call** and change its argument:

Method `TakeDamage (single)` of `Character`, template **Method script**, **Before the call**:

```js
// Before Character.TakeDamage(amount): ctx.this is the character hit.
if (ctx.this.IsPlayer)
  ctx.args.amount = 0;
```

- `ctx.this` is the object the method runs on – here the `Character` being hit.
- `ctx.args.amount = 0` changes the argument before the method sees it. `TakeDamage` then subtracts 0.
- Enemies are hit normally, because for them `IsPlayer` is `false`.

The message log now reports 0 damage for hits on the player, next to the base damage that would have hit. Your own hits on enemies count in full.

### Double experience

Method `AddExperience (double)` of `Character`, **Method script**, before the call:

```js
if (ctx.this.IsPlayer)
  ctx.args.amount = ctx.args.amount * 2;
```

Kill a goblin: instead of 10.25 the player gains 20.5 experience, and level-ups come twice as fast – the game's own `LevelUp` runs as usual, because the hook changed what `AddExperience` received, not the stored value.

For `AddGold (int)` the same idea needs whole numbers, because the parameter is an `int`:

```js
ctx.args.amount = Math.round(ctx.args.amount * 1.5);
```

## Value hook or method hook?

| Goal | Better |
| --- | --- |
| Multiply, fix or clamp one value | Value hook – simplest, and works in any game |
| Treat player and enemies differently | Method hook on `CalculateDamage` or `TakeDamage`, checking `IsPlayer` |
| Change what a method works with (its arguments) | Method hook, before the call |
| Survive a new game without a pointer chain | Method hook – it catches the method, whichever objects it is called for |

Both kinds are stored per program and reinstalled the next time you attach to HermesQuest. They can be paused, debugged and removed in the **Hooks** tab.

```

`docs/examples/hermesquest-scans.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest: scans and pointer scan

Start [HermesQuest](index.md), attach to it with **Select process** (`HermesQuest.x86_64`, or `HermesQuest.exe` under Wine/Proton) and keep the **F1** view of the game at hand: it shows every value exactly.

The [scanning guide](../guide/scanning.md) explains the scan types; here they are applied to a game whose values behave like those of real games.

## Gold: an exact integer

Gold starts at 0, and searching for 0 finds millions of addresses. So earn some first:

1. Press **2** to spawn a goblin and walk into it until it dies. The log says how much gold it dropped, e.g. "You gain 10.25 experience and 5 gold."
2. In Hermes choose the data type `int32`, scan type **Exact value**, enter the gold (`5`) and click **First scan**.
3. Kill another enemy, enter the new amount and click **Next scan**. After two or three rounds one address is left.
4. **Track** it and call it "Gold".

!!! tip "Why `int32`?"
    `Gold` is declared as `int` in the game's C# code, which is always 4 bytes. If you don't know the type, **Guess automatically** tries `int32`, `int64`, `float` and `double` at once.

## Mana: a float that changes on its own

Mana is a `float` that regenerates by 0.13 per second in real time. Between two scans it changes, even if you do nothing – exactly what makes values like stamina or energy bars hard to find in real games.

1. Spawn a rat (**1**) next to you and press **F**: Fire Bolt costs 7.5 mana. The panel beside the map shows mana with one decimal place, e.g. `MP 42.5/50`.
2. Data type `float`, **Exact value** `42.5`, float comparison **Rounded**. "Rounded" finds every value that shows as 42.5 with one decimal place (42.45 to 42.55), whatever the hidden decimals are. With **Exact** you would only find it within the same frame.
3. Spawn another rat and cast again. Scan **Decreased by …** `7.5` with tolerance `0.5`: the tolerance absorbs the mana that regenerated between the two scans. Don't wait long between casting and scanning – 0.5 mana regenerate in under four seconds.
4. Wait a few seconds and scan **Increased** – only mana grows by itself.
5. Track the address and call it "Mana".

Tracked, the value visibly counts up in the address list until it reaches 50.

## Experience: a double

`Experience` is a `double` (8 bytes). Enemies bring uneven amounts: a rat 4.5, a goblin 10.25, a skeleton 15.5.

1. Data type `double`, **Exact value** with the experience the F1 view shows, e.g. `14.75`.
2. Kill a skeleton (**3**), then **Increased by …** `15.5`, without tolerance: whole kills are exact.

!!! question "Why does `float` not find it?"
    A `double` and a `float` with the same value have entirely different bytes. A scan with the wrong type finds nothing – or, for small integers, chance hits. When a value shows decimals that don't fit, try the other floating-point type.

## Pointer scan: surviving "New game"

Press **N**: the game builds a new player, and all tracked addresses now point into memory the game no longer uses. A **pointer chain** finds the value again. Mana is a good target, because you can find it again right after a new game.

1. Right-click "Mana" → **Find pointers …**.
2. Untick **Only chains starting in HermesQuest.x86_64**. In a Unity game the program file is only a small launcher; the chains start in the Mono runtime (`libmonobdwgc-2.0.so`, or `mono-2.0-bdwgc.dll` on Windows) or in `UnityPlayer`.
3. Click **New scan**. It finds many candidates.
4. Press **N** in the game. Find mana again as above: spawn a rat, cast, **Exact value** `42.5` rounded, then **Decreased by …** `7.5` ± `0.5`.
5. In the pointer dialog click **Take from scan**, then **Filter with this address**. Chains that only matched by chance drop out.
6. Repeat steps 4 and 5 once or twice. Then pick the shortest remaining chain and click **Use pointer**.

From now on "Mana" resolves after every new game and every restart of HermesQuest.

!!! tip "How to read a chain"
    The game reaches mana as `GameState.Current → Player → Stats → Mana`. The last offsets of a good chain are exactly these steps: the offset of `Player` in `GameState`, of `Stats` in `Character` and of `Mana` in `CharacterStats`. The object inspector shows each field's offset (see [Unity (Mono)](../engines/unity-mono.md)), so you can check a chain against the game's own structure. What comes before is the way from the Mono runtime to the static field `GameState.Current`.

!!! note "No chain found?"
    Raise **Max. depth** by one or two. Managed games often need deeper chains than native ones, because the way to a static field leads through the runtime's own tables.

With the chain in place you can give **Gold** and **Experience** chains too: they differ from Mana's only in the last offset, because all three are fields of the same `CharacterStats` object. Hermes does not derive them for you: scan for each, then filter its pointer scan as above.

## A shortcut for Mono games

For scripts and method hooks you need no pointer chain at all: they reach the player through the game's own static field, `GameState.Current`, which is always right – see [Scripts](hermesquest-scripts.md). Pointer chains matter for tracked addresses, freezing and value hooks.

```

`docs/examples/hermesquest-scripts.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest: scripts

[Scripts](../guide/scripts.md) are JavaScript that Hermes runs on the game's main thread, by hand or on a timer. They read and change the game's objects through their fields and call its methods – no addresses, no pointer chains. This page builds up from reading one value to scripts with parameters. If JavaScript is new to you, keep [JavaScript in Hermes](javascript.md) open beside it.

To create a script: attach to HermesQuest, open the **Scripts** tab, click **New …**, give it a name, choose **When** it runs, and type the code. **Run now** runs the selected script at once; what it logs and returns appears in the log below the scripts.

## The way in: `GameState.Current`

In a Unity game, `ctx.find("ClassName")` finds Unity objects – GameObjects and components. HermesQuest keeps its state in plain C# objects, which Unity does not know about. Their entry point is a **static field**: `GameState.Current`, the running game. `ctx.static` reads it:

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
```

`"HermesQuest.GameState.Current"` is namespace, class and field. The result is an object you can walk through like in C#: `game.Player` is the player, `game.Player.Stats` its stats. Because the script asks for `GameState.Current` every time it runs, it always finds the current game – also after "New game", where tracked addresses need a pointer chain.

## 1. Show the character

**When:** Only when run by hand.

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
const player = game.Player;
const stats = player.Stats;

ctx.log(`Level ${stats.Level}, turn ${game.Turn}, ${game.Kills} kills`);
ctx.log(`Health ${stats.Health.toFixed(1)} / ${stats.MaxHealth}`);
ctx.log(`Mana   ${stats.Mana.toFixed(1)} / ${stats.MaxMana}`);
ctx.log(`Gold   ${stats.Gold}, experience ${stats.Experience}`);

return player;
```

- `const` gives a value a name for the rest of the script.
- Text in backticks `` `…` `` is a *template*: `${…}` inserts a value. `toFixed(1)` rounds a number to one decimal place for display.
- `ctx.log(…)` writes a line to the script log.
- `return player` makes the player the script's result. The log shows it as a link: click it to open the player in the **object inspector**, with all its fields.

## 2. Heal fully – two ways

**When:** Only when run by hand.

Writing the fields directly:

```js
const stats = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats;
stats.Health = stats.MaxHealth;
stats.Mana = stats.MaxMana;
```

Assigning to a field (`stats.Health = …`) writes the new value straight into the game's memory. The game does not notice that anything happened.

Calling the game's own method:

```js
const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
const healed = player.Heal(1000);
return `Healed ${healed.toFixed(1)} health`;
```

`player.Heal(1000)` runs the game's method `Character.Heal` with the argument 1000. That method follows the game's rules – it never heals above the maximum – and returns how much it healed, which the script shows as its result.

!!! tip "Field or method?"
    Writing a field is direct and works for every value. Calling a method lets the game do the work with its own rules: limits, side effects, messages. When the game has a method for what you want, prefer it.

## 3. Regenerate on a timer

**When:** Repeatedly, every 5 seconds.

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
if (game === null || game.GameOver)
  return;

const healed = game.Player.Heal(1);
if (healed > 0)
  ctx.log(`+${healed} health`);
```

- `if (…) return;` ends this run early: before the first game exists (`null`) or when the player is dead.
- `||` means *or*. `game.GameOver` is a `bool` field of the game.
- Logging only when something happened keeps the log readable – a repeating script runs hundreds of times.

The next run starts five seconds after the previous one *ended*, so runs never overlap.

## 4. Stronger player, kept after "New game"

**When:** Repeatedly, every 2 seconds. **Parameters:** two numbers, `outgoing` (default `2`) and `incoming` (default `0.5`).

`Combat.CalculateDamage` multiplies every hit by the attacker's `DamageOutgoingMultiplier` and the target's `DamageIncomingMultiplier`. Setting them on the player is the game's own way to make it stronger – but "New game" creates a new player with both back at 1. A repeating script puts them back:

```js
const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
const wanted = { DamageOutgoingMultiplier: ctx.args.outgoing,
                 DamageIncomingMultiplier: ctx.args.incoming };

for (const [field, value] of Object.entries(wanted)) {
  if (Math.abs(player[field] - value) > 0.0001) {
    player[field] = value;
    ctx.log(`${field} set to ${value}`);
  }
}
```

- `ctx.args.outgoing` is the value of the parameter `outgoing`. A timed run uses the parameter's default; **Run now** asks for the values.
- `{ name: value, … }` is a JavaScript object; `Object.entries` turns it into pairs, and `for (const [field, value] of …)` walks through them.
- `player[field]` is the same as `player.DamageOutgoingMultiplier` when `field` holds that name: square brackets take the field's name from a variable.
- `Math.abs(a - b) > 0.0001` compares floating-point numbers. The game stores `float`, JavaScript calculates with `double`; a value like 0.3 is not exactly equal in both, so `!==` would report a difference every time.

The message log of the game shows the multipliers in every hit, e.g. `(base 5 x2 x1)`.

## 5. Gold on demand

**When:** Only when run by hand. **Parameter:** a number `amount`, default `100`.

```js
const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
const amount = Math.trunc(ctx.args.amount);
player.AddGold(amount);
return `${amount} gold added, now ${player.Stats.Gold}`;
```

`AddGold` takes an `int`; `Math.trunc` cuts off decimals someone may have typed. Run it with **Run now**: Hermes asks for the amount first.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="560" }
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-light.webp#only-light){ width="560" }
  <figcaption>A manual run asks for the script's parameters (here a script of another game).</figcaption>
</figure>

## 6. Train an attribute – a choice parameter

**When:** Only when run by hand. **Parameters:** a choice `attribute` and a number `points` (default `1`).

The choice gets its options from a short piece of code. For `attribute`:

```js
return [
  { label: "Strength (melee damage)", value: "Strength" },
  { label: "Dexterity (hit chance)", value: "Dexterity" },
  { label: "Intelligence (Fire Bolt damage)", value: "Intelligence" },
];
```

The list shows the labels; the script gets the value. The script:

```js
const stats = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats;
const name = ctx.args.attribute;          // "Strength", "Dexterity" or "Intelligence"
const before = stats[name];
stats[name] = before + Math.trunc(ctx.args.points);
return `${name}: ${before} → ${stats[name]}`;
```

The options code runs in the game too, so it could also read them from it – for example the names of the enemies around. Here a fixed list is enough.

## 7. The nearest enemy

**When:** Only when run by hand.

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
const player = game.Player;
const enemy = game.NearestEnemy(player, 8);
if (enemy === null)
  return "No enemy within 8 steps";

const chance = ctx.call("HermesQuest.Combat:HitChance", player, enemy);
ctx.log(`${enemy.Name}: ${enemy.Stats.Health} health, hit chance ${Math.round(chance * 100)} %`);

enemy.Stats.Health = 1;
return enemy;
```

- `game.NearestEnemy(player, 8)` calls a method of the game object and passes the player object along; the game returns a `Character` or `null`.
- `ctx.call("HermesQuest.Combat:HitChance", …)` calls a **static** method – one that belongs to a class, not to an object. The name is written as the catalog shows it: `Namespace.Class:Method`.
- `enemy.Stats.Health = 1` leaves the enemy at one health point; the next hit kills it.

## 8. Remember between runs: `ctx.state`

**When:** Repeatedly, every 10 seconds.

```js
const gold = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats.Gold;

if (ctx.state.lastGold !== undefined && gold > ctx.state.lastGold)
  ctx.log(`+${gold - ctx.state.lastGold} gold in the last 10 seconds`);

ctx.state.lastGold = gold;
```

Variables declared with `const` exist for one run only. `ctx.state` is an object that the script keeps while Hermes stays attached, also when you edit the code: whatever the script stores in it is there again on the next run. On the first run `ctx.state.lastGold` does not exist yet – it is `undefined` – which the `if` checks before comparing.

## When something goes wrong

- **An error** stops the run and appears in the log with its message, e.g. for a misspelt field: *HermesQuest.CharacterStats has no field Helth*. The script stays and runs again at its next time.
- **`null`**: before the game has created its state, or for an enemy that is gone, a field or method returns `null`. Check with `if (x === null)` before using it.
- **Names are case-sensitive**: `stats.health` is not `stats.Health`. The object inspector (open it from a returned object) shows the exact names.
- **Long loops freeze the game**: a script runs on the game's main thread, and the game waits until it ends. Keep scripts short and never write a loop that waits for something in the game – use a repeating script instead (its interval must be above 0).

```

`docs/examples/index.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest

HermesQuest is a small role-playing game made for trying out Hermes Hook. It is a Unity game with the Mono backend, so every tool works on it: value scans, pointer scans, the write watch, value hooks, and the [Unity (Mono)](../engines/unity-mono.md) tools – catalog, trace, method monitor, method hooks and scripts. The examples in this section all use it.

It is deliberately built like a real game: the values live in heap objects behind pointers, "New game" moves them to new addresses, player and enemies share one class, and all damage goes through one pipeline that hooks and scripts can change.

## Download

| System | Download |
| --- | --- |
| Linux (native, x86-64) | [HermesQuest-RPG-Linux](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/releases/download/v0.5.0-alpha/HermesQuest-RPG-Linux) |
| Windows, or Linux under Wine/Proton | [HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip](https://github.com/winterhafen/hermes-hook/releases/download/v0.5.0-alpha/HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip) |

Both are zip archives with the game folder in them. The Linux file has no `.zip` extension, but unpacks the same way.

=== "Linux"

    ```bash
    unzip HermesQuest-RPG-Linux -d HermesQuest
    ./HermesQuest/Linux/HermesQuest.x86_64
    ```

    In Hermes the game shows up as `HermesQuest.x86_64`. Remember the [permissions](../getting-started/permissions.md): with `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` at `1`, Hermes cannot reach a game it did not start.

=== "Windows"

    Unpack `HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip` and start `Windows\HermesQuest.exe`. In Hermes it shows up as `HermesQuest.exe`.

=== "Under Wine/Proton"

    The Windows build is also the test case for [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md):

    ```bash
    unzip HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip -d HermesQuest
    wine ./HermesQuest/Windows/HermesQuest.exe
    ```

    or add `HermesQuest.exe` to Steam as a non-Steam game and start it with Proton. The first time you select it, Hermes offers to download Frida's Windows gadget.

`-seed <n>` on the command line fixes the map and every roll, also after "New game", so a run can be repeated exactly:

```bash
./HermesQuest/Linux/HermesQuest.x86_64 -seed 42
```

  ![HermesQuest](../assets/photos/hermesquest-map.webp)

## Playing

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Arrows, WASD, numpad | Move; walk into an enemy to attack it |
| Space / R | Wait / rest (recover 2 health) |
| F | Fire Bolt at the nearest enemy, costs 7.5 mana |
| E, 1–5 | Spawn a random enemy / a rat, goblin, skeleton, orc or ogre |
| Delete | Remove all enemies |
| C | Character sheet |
| F1 | Debug view with the exact values and the process ID |
| H | Help |
| N | New game |

Enemies only appear when you spawn them, so you decide when a fight starts. Killing one brings experience and gold:

| Enemy | Key | Health | Experience | Gold |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rat | 1 | 6 | 4.5 | 0–2 |
| Goblin | 2 | 12 | 10.25 | 3–8 |
| Skeleton | 3 | 18 | 15.5 | 2–10 |
| Orc | 4 | 28 | 24.75 | 8–20 |
| Ogre | 5 | 60 | 60 | 20–45 |

The **F1** view shows every value with all its decimal places – handy to check what a scan should find – and the process ID to pick the right process in Hermes.

## How the game is built

This is what the examples rely on. All code is in the namespace `HermesQuest`; the catalog shows it in the assembly `Assembly-CSharp`.

### The values

```text
GameState.Current            static field: the running game
  └─ Player                  Character
       ├─ Stats              CharacterStats
       │    ├─ Level         int
       │    ├─ Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence   int
       │    ├─ Health, MaxHealth                   float
       │    ├─ Mana, MaxMana                       float
       │    ├─ Experience                          double
       │    └─ Gold                                int
       ├─ DamageOutgoingMultiplier                 float, 1.0
       └─ DamageIncomingMultiplier                 float, 1.0
```

- The player starts with 50 health, 50 mana, 0 experience and 0 gold.
- **Mana regenerates by 0.13 per second** in real time, also while the game is in the background. A value that changes on its own is a good test for scans with tolerance.
- **Experience is a double** with decimals (a goblin brings 10.25), shown rounded on the character sheet.
- **New game** builds a new `GameState` with a new player and new stats: all addresses change, as after loading a save game in a real game.

### The damage pipeline

Melee attacks and Fire Bolt, of the player and of enemies, all go through the same methods:

```text
Combat.MeleeAttack / Combat.CastFireBolt
  └─ Combat.ApplyDamage(game, attacker, target, baseDamage, source)
       ├─ Combat.CalculateDamage(attacker, target, baseDamage)
       │      returns baseDamage × attacker.DamageOutgoingMultiplier
       │                         × target.DamageIncomingMultiplier
       └─ Character.TakeDamage(amount)      writes target.Stats.Health
```

- Player and enemies are both `Character`; `IsPlayer` tells them apart. A hook on `TakeDamage` therefore hits everyone unless it checks `IsPlayer`.
- The message log shows base damage and multipliers of every hit, and the F1 view the last calculation, so you see at once what a hook or script changed.
- Every method that writes a value has a method of its own: `TakeDamage`, `Heal`, `SpendMana`, `RegenerateMana`, `AddGold`, `AddExperience`. They are compiled without inlining, so each is a separate function in memory that the write watch names and that a hook can catch.

## The examples

1. [Scans and pointer scan](hermesquest-scans.md): find gold, mana and experience, and a pointer chain that survives a new game.
2. [Hooks](hermesquest-hooks.md): multiply gold at the instruction that writes it, protect the player but not the enemies, change damage with method hooks.
3. [Scripts](hermesquest-scripts.md): read and change the character from JavaScript, heal on a timer, scripts with parameters.
4. [JavaScript in Hermes](javascript.md): the language as far as hooks and scripts need it, explained along the examples.

If you have never used Hermes, do the [tutorial](../getting-started/first-hook.md) with the small C test game first; it explains the main window step by step.

`docs/examples/javascript.md`:

```md
# JavaScript in Hermes

Hermes uses JavaScript wherever you tell it *what* to do with a value or with the game: hook templates, method hooks and scripts. You need little of the language for that. This page explains that part, along the [HermesQuest](index.md) examples – no previous knowledge of JavaScript assumed.

## Where JavaScript is used

| Where | Shape | Runs | Gets | Its `return` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Hook template](../guide/templates.md) (value hook) | a **function**: `ctx => …` or `function (ctx) { … }` | after every hooked write, in the writing thread | `ctx.old`, `ctx.new`, `ctx.delta`, `ctx.params`, `ctx.state` | the value to store; nothing keeps the game's value |
| [Method hook](hermesquest-hooks.md#method-hooks) with *Method script* | the **body** of a function: just the statements | before or after every call of the method | `ctx.args`, `ctx.this`, `ctx.result`, `ctx.phase`, `ctx.call`, `ctx.static`, `ctx.find` | after the call: the new result |
| [Script](hermesquest-scripts.md) | the **body** of a function | by hand or on a timer, on the game's main thread | `ctx.static`, `ctx.find`, `ctx.call`, `ctx.args`, `ctx.state`, `ctx.log` | shown as the script's result |
| Options of a choice parameter | the **body** of a function | when the run dialog asks for them | the same `ctx` as scripts | the list of options |

All of them get one object, `ctx` (for *context*), through which they reach everything else. The [hook context](../reference/hook-context.md) and [script context](../reference/script-context.md) references list its fields.

A **function** is code with a name for its input; a **body** is just the code inside. A template is a function because Hermes stores and tests it on its own; a script is a body because Hermes wraps it into a function for you:

```js
// A function (hook template): input ctx, result after =>
ctx => ctx.new * 2

// A body (script): statements, ctx is simply there
const stats = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats;
return stats.Gold;
```

## Statements, comments and names

A script is a list of **statements**, run from top to bottom. A statement usually ends with `;` – JavaScript tolerates missing ones, but writing them avoids surprises.

```js
// A comment: from // to the end of the line, ignored.
/* A longer comment
   over several lines. */

const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
let healed = 0;
healed = player.Heal(5);
```

- `const name = value;` gives a value a name. It cannot be given another value later – use it by default.
- `let name = value;` is the same, but may change later (`healed = …`).
- Names are **case-sensitive**: `player` and `Player` are different, and so are the game's fields – `Stats.Health`, never `stats.health`.

## Values

### Numbers

JavaScript has one number type: a 64-bit floating-point number (C#'s `double`). Hermes converts the game's types for you:

| Game type | In JavaScript | Watch out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int`, `short`, `byte` … | number | When writing one back, cut decimals off with `Math.trunc` or `Math.round`. In value hooks Hermes truncates integer results itself. |
| `long` (`int64`) | number | Exact only up to 2^53 (about 9 × 10^15). |
| `float` | number | The game keeps only about 7 significant digits. |
| `double` | number | Same precision as JavaScript. |

Calculating works as expected: `+ - * /`, `%` for the remainder, parentheses for order. Useful functions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `Math.round(x)`, `Math.trunc(x)`, `Math.floor(x)`, `Math.ceil(x)` | round, cut off, round down, round up |
| `Math.min(a, b)`, `Math.max(a, b)` | the smaller, the larger value |
| `Math.abs(x)` | the value without its sign |
| `x.toFixed(2)` | `x` as text with two decimal places, for display |

!!! warning "Comparing floats"
    `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false` in JavaScript, as in almost every language: most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly. A `float` from the game, read into JavaScript's `double`, is a little off as well. Compare with a tolerance instead:

    ```js
    if (Math.abs(stats.Mana - 42.5) < 0.001) …
    ```

### Text

Text (a *string*) is written in quotes: `"Hero"` or `'Hero'`. For text with values in it, use backticks and `${…}`:

```js
ctx.log(`${enemy.Name} has ${enemy.Stats.Health.toFixed(1)} health`);
// Goblin has 7.5 health
```

### True and false

Comparisons give `true` or `false`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `a === b`, `a !== b` | equal, not equal |
| `a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b`, `a >= b` | smaller, greater … |
| `x && y` | `x` **and** `y` |
| `x \|\| y` | `x` **or** `y` |
| `!x` | **not** `x` |

Always use `===` and `!==`. The shorter `==` converts values before comparing (`"1" == 1` is `true`), which hides mistakes.

### Nothing: `null` and `undefined`

- `null` means *no object*: `game.NearestEnemy(player, 8)` gives `null` when no enemy is near, `ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current")` before the first game exists.
- `undefined` means *not set*: a field of `ctx.state` you have not stored yet, or a function that ends without `return`.

Using a field of `null` is an error (`cannot read property 'Stats' of null`), so check first:

```js
const enemy = game.NearestEnemy(player, 8);
if (enemy === null)
  return "No enemy near";
ctx.log(enemy.Name);
```

## Decisions: `if`

```js
if (ctx.args.attacker.IsPlayer) {
  return ctx.result * 3;
} else if (ctx.args.target.IsPlayer) {
  return ctx.result / 2;
} else {
  ctx.log("enemy against enemy");
}
```

The block in `{ … }` runs only if the condition in `( … )` is `true`. With a single statement the braces may be left out, as in the [hooks examples](hermesquest-hooks.md#only-the-player-hits-harder-and-takes-less).

`return` ends the script (or function) at once. Everything after it is skipped – that is how `if (game === null) return;` stops a script early.

## Arrow functions and the conditional operator

Hook templates are usually one line:

```js
ctx => ctx.delta < 0 ? ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2 : ctx.new
```

Two pieces of syntax do the work:

- `ctx => …` is an **arrow function**: it takes `ctx` and gives back what follows the arrow.
- `condition ? a : b` is the **conditional operator**: `a` if the condition is true, else `b`.

So the template reads: *take `ctx`; if the value went down, give back the old value plus half the change, otherwise the value the game wrote.* With the player at 40 health and a hit of 6 the game writes 34; `ctx.delta` is −6, and the hook stores 40 + (−6 / 2) = 37.

The same in the long form, which can hold several statements:

```js
function (ctx) {
  if (ctx.delta < 0)
    return ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2;
  return ctx.new;
}
```

Both forms are fine for templates. Returning nothing (`undefined`) or `null` keeps what the game wrote.

## Lists and objects

A **list** (array) holds values in order, in square brackets; an **object** holds named values, in braces:

```js
const names = ["Strength", "Dexterity", "Intelligence"];
names[0]          // "Strength" – counting starts at 0
names.length      // 3

const option = { label: "Strength (melee damage)", value: "Strength" };
option.label      // "Strength (melee damage)"
```

Going through all entries of a list:

```js
for (const name of names)
  ctx.log(`${name}: ${stats[name]}`);
```

`stats[name]` reads the field whose name is in the variable `name` – the same as `stats.Strength` when `name` is `"Strength"`.

`ctx.state` is such an object. Store what a hook or script should remember in it:

```js
ctx.state.calls = (ctx.state.calls || 0) + 1;
```

`(ctx.state.calls || 0)` is the stored count, or 0 the first time, when it is still `undefined`.

## Game objects

What `ctx.static`, `ctx.find`, `ctx.args`, `ctx.this` or a method give you for an object of the game is a **wrapper**: a JavaScript object that reads from and writes to the game's memory each time you use it.

| You write | Hermes does |
| --- | --- |
| `player.Stats` | reads the field `Stats` – an object again |
| `stats.Health` | reads the field `Health` from the game's memory, now |
| `stats.Health = 50` | writes 50 into the field |
| `player.IsDead` | runs the property's getter `get_IsDead` in the game |
| `player.Heal(10)` | calls the method `Heal` with 10 and gives its result |
| `ctx.call("HermesQuest.Combat:HitChance", player, enemy)` | calls a static method; objects can be passed along |
| `ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current")` | reads a static field |
| `player.className` | the object's class, `"HermesQuest.Character"` |

Because every read goes to the game, a value read twice may differ – mana regenerates between the two reads. Read it once into a `const` if you need it several times.

The wrapper's own names come first: `name`, `className`, `field`, `get`, `call`, and in Unity `component`. If the game has a field of one of these names, read it with `obj.field("name")`.

!!! tip "Finding the names"
    Return an object from a script, or click an object in the method monitor: the **object inspector** lists its fields, properties and methods with their exact names and types. The [catalog](../engines/index.md#catalog) lists every class and method.

## Finding mistakes

- **`ctx.log(…)`** writes to the script log; in hooks to the hook log below the Hooks tab and to the debug window. Log values to see what the code works with: `ctx.log(ctx.old, ctx.new, ctx.delta)`.
- **Test** in the template editor runs a value template without the game: enter old and new value and see what it stores. It runs in Qt's JavaScript engine, so Frida's functions (`ptr`, `Memory`) are missing there.
- **Debug** in the Hooks tab logs every call of the selected hooks with old value, game value, result, log output and errors.
- **Errors** appear with their message in the log. A value hook whose script fails keeps the game's value; a script that fails stops this run only.

## Things to remember

- Scripts and method hooks run **inside the game**, on its thread: keep them short. A loop that waits for something blocks the game.
- A value hook runs at **every write** of its instruction, possibly thousands of times a second. Avoid `ctx.log` there except while debugging.
- Writing a field bypasses the game's rules; calling its method follows them.
- After "New game" every object is new. Scripts that ask `ctx.static(…)` each run find the new ones by themselves.

```

`docs/getting-started/first-hook.md`:

```md
# Tutorial: your first hook

This tutorial uses the small test game in the repository to go through the whole path once: find the gold, see which code changes it, and hook that code so every gold gain is ten times as large. It takes about ten minutes.

## The test game

`test_app/dummy_game.c` is a minimal GTK game with buttons for **Gold +100**, **Gold −100** and **New game**, plus mana, experience and a treasure hunt for trying [fuzzy scans](../guide/scanning.md#fuzzy-scans). As in real games, the player lives on the heap behind pointers (`g_game → player → gold`), so the address of the gold changes with every start and every **New game**. The game prints its PID, the pointer chain and the current address of the gold to the terminal, so you can check what Hermes finds. Several instances may run at once.

Build and start it (needs `gcc` and the GTK 3 development packages: `gtk3-devel` on Fedora, `libgtk-3-dev` on Debian/Ubuntu):

```bash
mkdir -p build
gcc -O2 test_app/dummy_game.c -o build/dummy_game.exe $(pkg-config --cflags --libs gtk+-3.0)
./build/dummy_game.exe
```

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hermes Hook next to the test game](../assets/photos/dummy-game-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hermes Hook next to the test game](../assets/photos/dummy-game-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Where this tutorial leads: the test game on the right, Hermes on the left with its gold found and tracked through a pointer chain.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 1. Attach to the game

Click **Select process** in Hermes and choose `dummy_game.exe`. The toolbar and the status bar now show the program, its PID and whether it is 32 or 64 bit.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Process selection](../assets/screenshots/process-list-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Process selection](../assets/screenshots/process-list-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
  <figcaption>Select process lists the running programs; Wine/Proton games appear as their Windows program.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 2. Find the gold

1. Enter the gold shown in the game as **Search value**, keep the data type `int32` and click **First scan**. Thousands of addresses hold that number by chance.
2. Click **Gold +100** in the game, enter the new value and click **Next scan**. Repeat until one or a few addresses are left.
3. Select the address and click **Track** (or double-click it). Give it a description such as "Gold".

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Main window after scanning](../assets/screenshots/main-window-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Main window after scanning](../assets/screenshots/main-window-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>After two scans three addresses are left; the gold is tracked below.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 3. See which code writes it

Right-click "Gold" in the tracked addresses and choose **Address watch (writes)**. Click **Gold +100** in the game: the watch window lists the code location that raised the gold, e.g. `dummy_game.exe+0x…`. **Gold −100** produces a second row of its own.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Write watch](../assets/screenshots/write-watch-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Write watch](../assets/screenshots/write-watch-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The write watch lists each code location that wrote the gold, how often, and whether it reads or writes the value.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 4. Hook it

Select the row of the increase and click **Create hook**. Choose the template **Multiplier**, factor `10`, and "Increases only".

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Create hook dialog](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Create hook dialog](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
  <figcaption>The hook dialog builds its form from the parameters of the chosen template.</figcaption>
</figure>

The hook appears in the **Hooks** tab. Every click on **Gold +100** now brings 1000 gold; the column **Last** shows the old value → the value the game wrote ⇒ the value stored.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Active hooks with their template, target and last call.</figcaption>
</figure>

In the **Hooks** tab hooks can be edited, paused, debugged and removed. When a hook is removed, when you select another process and when Hermes exits, the original bytes of the game are restored.

## 5. Make it last

Restart the game, or click **New game**: the gold now lives at another address. For the tracked address and the hook to find it again, give "Gold" a pointer chain with the [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md). From then on both follow the gold after every restart, and Hermes installs the hook again by itself whenever you attach to the game.

## Where next

- [Scanning](../guide/scanning.md) explains every scan type, including tolerance and rounded floats with the game's mana and experience.
- [Hooks](../guide/hooks.md) explains how a hook works, what happens after a restart, and its limitations.
- [Hook templates](../guide/templates.md) shows how to write manipulations of your own in JavaScript.

```md
# Installation

## Requirements

- GNU/Linux or Windows on x86-64
- Python 3.11 or newer, with `venv` and `pip`
- On Linux a graphical session with X11 or Wayland

On Debian or Ubuntu, Python and the tools come from the distribution if needed:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip
```

The Python dependencies, PySide6 among them, are installed with `pip` from `pyproject.toml`. If Qt reports a missing platform plugin at start, add the distribution's Qt/XCB runtime packages.

## Install

In the project directory:

=== "Linux"

    ```bash
    python3 -m venv .venv
    source .venv/bin/activate
    python -m pip install --upgrade pip
    python -m pip install -e .
    ```

=== "Windows"

    ```powershell
    py -m venv .venv
    .venv\Scripts\activate
    python -m pip install --upgrade pip
    python -m pip install -e .
    ```

The editable install also sets up the console command `hermes`.

## Start

With the virtual environment activated:

```bash
hermes
```

Or straight from the project directory, without activating anything:

```bash
./.venv/bin/python -m hermes
```

### Menu entry and shortcut

=== "Linux"

    `scripts/hermes-hook.sh` activates the virtual environment (`.venv` in the project, or `$HERMES_VENV`) and starts Hermes from any working directory. A menu entry for the current user (KDE, GNOME, …) appears under Development and Games:

    ```bash
    ./scripts/install-desktop-entry.sh              # install or update the entry
    ./scripts/install-desktop-entry.sh --uninstall  # remove it
    ```

    The entry points to the project directory, so run the script again after moving the repository.

=== "Windows"

    `scripts\hermes-hook.cmd` starts Hermes the same way. For the Start menu and the taskbar, install a shortcut for the current user, then right-click "Hermes Hook" in the Start menu and choose "Pin to taskbar":

    ```powershell
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install-windows-shortcut.ps1             # install or update
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install-windows-shortcut.ps1 -Uninstall  # remove it
    ```

## Language

The interface is German or English, depending on the system locale (English for any other locale). Choose it under **Settings → General …**, or for one start with an environment variable, which applies while the setting is "as the system":

```bash
HERMES_LANGUAGE=en hermes
HERMES_LANGUAGE=de hermes
```

## First start

At the first start Hermes creates its SQLite database, where it keeps addresses, hooks, templates, scripts and settings per game. [Files and environment](../reference/files.md) lists where it lives and how to move it.

On Linux, continue with the [permissions](permissions.md) Hermes needs to read another process's memory.

`docs/getting-started/permissions.md`:

```md
# Permissions on Linux

Scans and writes go through `/proc/<pid>/mem`; the write watch, hooks and the engine tools attach to the game through [Frida](https://frida.re) (or ptrace). Both are subject to Linux's protections, in particular Yama's `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope`:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Processes of the same user may be inspected. |
| `1` | Only one's own child processes. The default of many distributions. Hermes then cannot access a game started separately. |

Do not run Hermes as root just in case, and do not loosen `ptrace_scope` permanently system-wide. For a session a temporary change is enough; it lapses at the next reboot:

```bash
sudo sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0
```

The process list only shows processes whose information the current user may access.

!!! tip "Windows games under Wine or Proton"
    Frida cannot attach to Wine processes the usual way. Hermes loads Frida's Windows gadget into the game instead, which needs a one-time download. See [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md).

On Windows no extra permissions are needed for games running as the same user.

`docs/guide/addresses.md`:

```md
# Tracked addresses

The **Tracked addresses** tab keeps the addresses you work with, with a description, the type, the live value and, if found, a pointer chain. They are stored per program and loaded again the next time you attach to it.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Tracked addresses](../assets/screenshots/main-window-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Tracked addresses](../assets/screenshots/main-window-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Addresses with pointer chains (purple) resolve again after a restart; "HP" is frozen at 100.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Adding addresses

- **Track** in the scan results, or a double-click on a result.
- **+ Address …** for an address you know, e.g. from another tool.
- From the object inspector, the hooks tab and scripts, which can hand addresses over.

Double-click the description to rename an entry. If an address lies in the program's static memory (a global variable), Hermes stores it as module + offset right away; it stays valid after a restart without a pointer scan.

## Writing and freezing

**Write value** writes a new value into the game once.

**Freeze** holds the current value: Hermes writes it back every 100 ms. Clicking again releases it; **Write value** changes the frozen value. For entries with a pointer chain or a static address the frozen state is stored and still applies after the game restarts. Entries without a chain are released when they are loaded again, because their address need no longer be right then.

!!! question "Freeze or hook?"
    Freezing needs no write watch and works on any value, but may flicker briefly, since the game can change the value between two passes. A [hook](hooks.md) with the template *Fixed value* acts directly at the write instruction, so the game never sees another value.

## Context menu

A right-click on an entry offers:

- **Show in memory viewer**: the [memory](tools.md#memory-viewer) around the address.
- **Change description …** and **Change value …**.
- **Address watch (writes)** and **Address watch (all accesses)**: the [write and read watch](write-watch.md).
- **Find pointers …**: the [pointer scan](pointer-scan.md); **Remove pointer** drops a chain again.

Scan results offer the memory viewer and the two watches as well.

## After a restart

Without a pointer chain the stored address is usually wrong after the game restarts, and the entry shows a stale value. With a chain Hermes resolves it again; while it cannot (e.g. in the main menu, before a save is loaded) the address column shows `?`, and the entry resolves once the chain leads somewhere again.

```

`docs/guide/data.md`:

```md
# Saving, export and import

## What Hermes keeps per game

Hermes identifies a game by its program and keeps for it:

- tracked addresses with their pointer chains and frozen values,
- hooks and method hooks,
- scripts,
- favorites and the chosen assemblies,
- catalogs read from Unity and Unreal games (in a cache beside the database), so the catalog also opens offline.

Hook templates and settings are shared by all games. Everything lives in one SQLite database; [Files and environment](../reference/files.md) says where.

When the attached game exits, Hermes resets the window within a second: scans, watches, freezing and hooks stop; stored addresses and hooks are kept and loaded again the next time you attach.

## Export and import

**File → Export game data …** writes everything saved for a game to a JSON file: per program path its addresses, hooks, method hooks, favorites and scripts, plus the templates its hooks were created from. The candidate chains of pointer scans are only exported when you ask for them, since they can be large.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Export](../assets/screenshots/game-export-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Export](../assets/screenshots/game-export-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
</figure>

**File → Import game data …** puts the entries of a file into one saved program, whatever path they were exported from – useful when a game moved, or for another computer. It either replaces what the program holds or mixes the file's entries in, leaving out those it holds already. A template in the file is linked to a local one with the same name and code, otherwise added (under a new name if the name is taken).

## Cleaning up

- **File → Delete saved entries …** deletes chosen addresses, pointer scans, hooks, method hooks, favorites or scripts of saved programs, or the programs altogether.
- **File → Compact database …** frees the space of deleted entries (e.g. large pointer scans) that SQLite otherwise keeps in the file.

```

`docs/guide/hooks.md`:

```md
# Hooks

A hook intercepts every write at one instruction of the game and changes the value written: with a multiplier, a fixed value, bounds, or a JavaScript function of your own. Hooks are stored per program and installed again the next time it starts.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The Hooks tab with its log below the table.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Creating a hook

1. Find the instruction that writes the value with the [write watch](write-watch.md).
2. Select its row and click **Create hook**.
3. Choose a [template](templates.md) and fill in its parameters. The built-in ones are **Multiplier**, **Fixed value** and **Clamp**.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Create hook](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Create hook](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
</figure>

Further options in the dialog:

**Caller levels**
:   For hooks without a pointer chain: how many return addresses identify a caller that writes the target (default `1`, at most `4`, `off` learns no callers). See [after a restart](#after-a-restart).

**Hardware breakpoint (code unchanged)**
:   Leaves the game's code as it is and uses one of the debug registers instead. Useful where code must not change; some anti-tamper protections detect debug registers, though.

## The Hooks tab

Several hooks can be selected at once (Ctrl/Shift-click): **Pause**, **Debug** and **Remove** act on all of them, **Edit** on one. The status column tells whether a hook is active, paused, training or could not be installed; the column **Last** shows the last call as old value → value written by the game ⇒ value stored.

Below the table a log shows what hook scripts write with `ctx.log` or `console.log`, and the errors of hooks, also without debug mode (at most 100 lines per 0.1 s; more are counted as dropped).

When a hook is removed, when you select another process and when Hermes exits, the original bytes are restored.

## Debugging hooks

**Debug** puts the selected hooks into debug mode and opens the debug window. It logs every call with time, thread, address, caller, old value, game value, result, `ctx.log` output and errors with their stack. Writes the hook skips appear too, with the reason, such as "writes another address" or "caller not learned".

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hook debug window](../assets/screenshots/hook-debug-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hook debug window](../assets/screenshots/hook-debug-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

Debug mode costs time in the game; with very many calls the agent drops entries and only counts them. Closing the window ends debug mode.

## After a restart

Hooks are stored per program, as module + offset of the write instruction. When the program is attached again after a restart, Hermes installs the stored hooks automatically. If the bytes at that location changed, e.g. after an update of the game, the hook is not installed.

If the write instruction lies in no module – e.g. in Mono/Unity JIT code, which is generated anew and elsewhere at every start – it depends on the target:

- **With a pointer chain** the hook is stored with the bytes of the write instruction and the surrounding code. In Mono games it also remembers the C# method of the write: after a restart Mono compiles that method and the hook is installed in it right away. Otherwise, or if that fails, the hook is in **Training**: Hermes watches the chain's target with a hardware watchpoint of its own and installs the hook at the first write from matching code. It takes effect from the next write on. The tooltip of the status column shows how many writes from other code were discarded. At most three hooks can train at a time; hooks installed as a hardware breakpoint take one of these three slots each.
- **Without a pointer chain** the hook cannot be stored, because its target is unknown after a restart.

The original target address is no longer valid after a restart. How the hook recognises the right writes depends on how it was created:

- **With a pointer chain**: the hook resolves the chain at every write and only acts on the address it leads to at that moment. This is the most reliable variant.
- **Without a pointer chain**: while running, the hook learns the callers, i.e. the return addresses on the stack, that write the target address. After a restart it only acts on writes from these callers. More caller levels help when the player and other objects are changed through the same helper function. If a learned caller also writes other addresses, Hermes points it out.

## How a hook works

The write watch reports the instruction *after* the write (hardware watchpoints fire afterwards). From it Hermes determines the actual write instruction and replaces it with a jump into a code cave:

```text
before(regs)       save the old value if the instruction really writes the target address
<write instruction, relocated>
after(regs)        call the manipulation and store the result
<remaining relocated bytes>
jmp back
```

Since Hermes only works with the old and the new value, it does not matter whether the game uses `add [mem], reg`, `mov [mem], reg` or `sub`. If the same instruction is also used for other objects (e.g. the enemies' gold), the hook only acts on its target: the watched address, the address of its pointer chain or, after a restart without a chain, the learned callers. Several hooks can share a write instruction; they run in the order they were created.

`before` and `after` are C functions (a Frida CModule): they check the target address and, on Windows and under Wine, the learned callers, and run the built-in manipulations themselves, so a hooked write costs a fraction of a microsecond. On Linux the callers are checked in JavaScript. Only scripts of your own, debug mode, caller learning and pointer chains run in JavaScript. The agent's JavaScript runs one thread at a time: a game thread that has to wait there can drop frames.

## Limitations

- x86-64 code only.
- The write instruction and the bytes up to the length of a jump (5 bytes) are overwritten. If other code jumps into the middle of this range, the game crashes; Frida hooks and Cheat Engine's code injection carry the same risk.
- If the write sits in a tiny function with less than 5 bytes before the next one, the setting *Hooks: short jump in tight spots* overwrites only 2 bytes with a short jump to `int3` padding nearby. The padding is found by a heuristic; if it guesses wrong, the game crashes.
- If the connection to Hermes breaks off unexpectedly while a hook is active, the game may crash.
- `int64` and `uint64` values are exact in manipulations only up to 2^53.
- Some games repair their code. The setting *patch hooks again that the game removed* reinstalls them (e.g. for Dark Souls III); see the [warning about anti-tamper systems](../index.md).

!!! tip "Hooks on methods"
    In Unity and Unreal games you can also hook a whole method instead of a single write: change its arguments, the fields of its object, or its result. See [method hooks](../engines/index.md#method-hooks).

```

# Native trace and monitor

When a game offers no engine metadata – or the logic you look for is plain C++ – the native tools work on machine code directly, for any engine.

## Native trace

**View → Native trace …** answers *which functions run when I do this?* It uses Frida's Stalker to count the functions the chosen threads call:

1. Record a **baseline** while the game idles.
2. Record a **scenario** while doing the thing you are interested in, e.g. paying gold.
3. The functions that are new in the scenario, or called more often there, are the candidates.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Native trace](../assets/screenshots/native-trace-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Native trace](../assets/screenshots/native-trace-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Candidates after a baseline and a scenario, with how often each ran.</figcaption>
</figure>

Candidates can be marked with ★ as [favorites](tools.md#favorites) or handed to the monitor.

!!! warning
    Stalker rewrites the code of the traced threads while it runs. Hermes asks before it starts, since this can slow down or, rarely, crash a game.

## Native function monitor

**Monitor native function …** logs the calls of one function: its arguments, the result and the caller. For pointer arguments it compares the memory behind them before and after the call, so you see what the function changed.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Native monitor](../assets/screenshots/native-monitor-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Native monitor](../assets/screenshots/native-monitor-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

Open it from a candidate of the native trace, from a favorite, or with an address you type in.

`docs/guide/pointer-scan.md`:

```md
# Pointer scan

Games keep most values on the heap, so their address changes with every start, every new game and often every level. What stays the same is the way there: a static pointer in the program, then a few offsets through the objects. The pointer scan finds these chains, e.g.

```
dummy_game.exe+0x4040 → 0x28 → 0x0
```

reads as: take the pointer at offset `0x4040` of the module `dummy_game.exe`, add `0x28` and read the pointer there, add `0x0` – that is the gold.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Pointer scan](../assets/screenshots/pointer-scan-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Pointer scan](../assets/screenshots/pointer-scan-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The pointer scan dialog with the chain of the test game and some chance hits.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Finding a chain

1. Right-click the tracked address → **Find pointers …** → **New scan**. In the test game it finds `dummy_game.exe+0x… → 0x28 → 0x0` (`g_game` → player → gold), plus some chance hits.
2. Make the value move: click **New game** (or restart the game) and find the value again in the scanner. The pointer dialog can stay open meanwhile.
3. Select the new result in the scanner, then **Take from scan** and **Filter with this address** in the pointer dialog. Chains that only matched because of the layout in memory drop out. A plain restart is often not enough for that, since the layout at start tends to be the same; a new game or a new level changes more.
4. Select the remaining chain → **Use pointer**.

From now on the tracked address resolves correctly after every restart, and hooks created from it follow the value too (see [hooks after a restart](hooks.md#after-a-restart)).

If the address lies in the program's static memory, no pointer scan is needed; the dialog says so.

!!! tip "Fewer, shorter chains"
    Prefer short chains from the game's own module over long ones through system libraries. When several chains survive filtering, keep the one with the fewest levels; repeat the filter step after a level change if in doubt.

```

`docs/guide/scanning.md`:

```md
# Scanning for values

The value search on the right of the main window finds the addresses where the game keeps a value. You narrow them down in steps: a **First scan** over the whole memory, then **Next scans** over the remaining results after the value changed in the game.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Value search](../assets/screenshots/main-window-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Value search](../assets/screenshots/main-window-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

## Data types

| Type | Size | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int8`, `uint8` | 1 byte | Flags, small counters |
| `int16`, `uint16` | 2 bytes | Older games, packed structures |
| `int32`, `uint32` | 4 bytes | The usual integer: gold, ammunition, levels |
| `int64`, `uint64` | 8 bytes | Large counters, money in some games |
| `float` | 4 bytes | Health, mana, positions, multipliers |
| `double` | 8 bytes | Experience, timers, values in managed games |

**Guess automatically** tries `int32`, `int64`, `float` and `double` at once. The smaller types match almost everywhere and have to be chosen explicitly.

**Aligned addresses only** skips addresses that are not a multiple of the type's size. Games almost always align their values, so the scan is faster and has fewer chance hits.

## Scan types

First scan:

| Scan type | Finds |
| --- | --- |
| Exact value | Addresses holding the value |
| Greater than / less than | Values above or below the number |
| Range | Values between two numbers |
| Unknown initial value | Every address; useful when the game shows no number, e.g. a health bar |

Next scan, compared with the previous scan:

| Scan type | Keeps addresses whose value |
| --- | --- |
| Changed / unchanged | changed or stayed the same |
| Increased / decreased | went up or down |
| Increased by … / decreased by … / changed by … | changed by the given amount |
| Exact value, greater, less, range | as in the first scan, against the current value |

!!! tip "Unknown values"
    For a health bar without a number: **Unknown initial value**, take damage, **Decreased**, wait, **Unchanged**, heal, **Increased** – a few rounds leave few addresses.

## Fuzzy scans

Games rarely show a value exactly as they store it. Two options help:

- **Tolerance (±)** for exact and by-X scans: `Increased by … 25` with tolerance `5` finds increases from 20 to 30.
- **Float comparison** for `float` and `double`: *Exact*, *Rounded* or *Truncated* to the decimal places you typed. `12.3` rounded finds 12.25 to 12.35.

The test game has examples of both:

- **Mana** (`float`, shown with one decimal place) regenerates by 0.13 every second; a spell costs 7.5. Scan **Exact value** with the value shown (e.g. `20.1`) and **Rounded**; with *Exact* the address is hard to find, because the stored value is e.g. 20.13. Then **Cast spell** and scan **Decreased by …** `7.5` with tolerance `0.5` – the regeneration between the scans would make a comparison without tolerance fail.
- **Experience** (`double`, shown without decimals): **Exact value** with the number shown and **Rounded**; after **Fight** scan **Increased by …** `12` with tolerance `3`.
- **Gold** (`int32`): after **Find treasure** scan **Increased by …** `25` with tolerance `5`.

## Taking results

Results show the address, type and live value. Select one or several and click **Track** (or double-click) to move them to the [tracked addresses](addresses.md). A right-click offers the memory viewer and the [write and read watch](write-watch.md) for a result directly.

The scan area folds away with **Hide address search** next to the tabs, **View → Address search** or ++ctrl+shift+f++; Hermes remembers the choice.

```

`docs/guide/scripts.md`:

```md
# Scripts

Scripts are JavaScript function bodies that run on the game's main thread and can call its methods: give the player health every few seconds, set an attribute after loading, or run a cheat function by hand. They live in the **Scripts** tab next to **Hooks**, are stored per program and restored when that program is attached. **New …** and **Edit** open the script editor with the code, the schedule and the parameters.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Scripts tab](../assets/screenshots/scripts-tab-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Scripts tab](../assets/screenshots/scripts-tab-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Scripts for an Unreal game with their schedule, and the script log below.</figcaption>
</figure>

Scripts reach game objects and methods through the engine adapters, so they need a [Unity or Unreal game](../engines/index.md).

## When a script runs

| Mode | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| **Once** | after the configured delay, each time the script starts |
| **Repeat** | every configured interval; the next interval starts after the previous run finished, so runs do not overlap |
| **Manual** | only when you click **Run now** |

## Parameters

Scripts can have parameters of the types text, number, yes/no or choice. A manual run asks for their values; scheduled runs use their defaults. The script reads them from `ctx.args`.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="560" }
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-light.webp#only-light){ width="560" }
</figure>

A choice parameter gets its options from a short JavaScript function evaluated in the game, returning values or `{label, value}` objects. The list filters as you type. The [Unreal page](../engines/unreal.md#example-a-script-with-a-choice-parameter) shows one in Gothic 1 Remake.

## Writing scripts

The script's `ctx` gives access to the game; all fields are in the [script context reference](../reference/script-context.md). Objects returned by `ctx.find` are wrappers: call instance methods with `.call(name, ...args)`, read fields and properties as properties, and use `.field(name)` where a name clashes. A returned object is shown as the result and can be opened in the object inspector.

```js title="Restore 50 health in Avowed (Unreal)"
ctx.find("AlabamaCheatManager").call("GiveHealth", 50);
```

```js title="Keep an attribute at a value (Unreal, Gameplay Ability System)"
const might = ctx.gas.get("Might");
if (might && might.base < 14) ctx.gas.setBase("AttributeSetCore.Might", 14);
```

```js title="Count runs and remember state"
ctx.state.total = (ctx.state.total || 0) + 1;
ctx.log(`run ${ctx.runs + 1}, total ${ctx.state.total}`);
```

Scripts are different from [hook templates](templates.md): a template changes one value at one write, a script runs on its own and calls the game.

```

# Settings and themes

## Settings

**Settings → General …** holds the settings, stored in Hermes' database.

`docs/guide/templates.md`:

```md
# Hook templates

A manipulation is a JavaScript function that runs in the game after every hooked write. It receives a `ctx` object and returns the value to store; `undefined` or `null` keeps the game's value. Integer results are truncated and limited to the range of the type.

```js title="The built-in Multiplier"
function (ctx) {
  const { factor, direction } = ctx.params;
  if (direction === 'increase' && ctx.delta <= 0)
    return undefined;
  if (direction === 'decrease' && ctx.delta >= 0)
    return undefined;
  return ctx.old + ctx.delta * factor;
}
```

The fields of `ctx` are listed in the [hook context reference](../reference/hook-context.md).

## Managing templates

Manipulations are stored in the database as **hook templates** and managed under **View → Hook templates …**. At first start Hermes creates the examples **Multiplier**, **Fixed value** and **Clamp**; they can be changed or deleted like templates of your own. Their texts are English whatever the language of the interface, since templates are data that exports share.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hook templates](../assets/screenshots/hook-templates-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hook templates](../assets/screenshots/hook-templates-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The built-in Multiplier with its parameters and its function.</figcaption>
</figure>

A template consists of a name, an optional description, the JavaScript function and parameters. Each parameter has

- a **name** – `ctx.params.<name>` in the script,
- a **label** shown in the hook dialog,
- a **type**: *Number*, *Choice* or *Code* for multi-line text,
- a **default**, and whether it is **optional**.

Choice values are written as `value=Label; value=Label`. The hook dialog builds its form from the parameters. A template with the number parameter `threshold` that only lets large gains through:

```js
ctx => ctx.delta >= ctx.params.threshold ? ctx.new : ctx.old
```

## Testing without a game

**Test** runs the function without a game process: enter the value type, the old value (`ctx.old`) and the value written by the game (`ctx.new`) and run it. It shows the stored value, the output of `ctx.log`/`console.log`, and errors. `ctx.state` is kept between test runs until it is reset.

!!! note
    The test runs in Qt's JavaScript engine rather than in Frida, so Frida APIs such as `ptr()` or `Memory` are not available there.

## Templates and existing hooks

A hook stores a **copy** of the template it was created from, so later changes to the template do not affect existing hooks. In the hook's **Edit** dialog Hermes points out a changed template and offers **Use changed template**. If the template is deleted, the hook keeps working with its copy.

## Examples

```js title="Never lose gold"
ctx => Math.max(ctx.new, ctx.old)
```

```js title="Count the calls and log every tenth"
ctx => {
  ctx.state.calls = (ctx.state.calls || 0) + 1;
  if (ctx.state.calls % 10 === 0) ctx.log(`call ${ctx.state.calls}: ${ctx.old} → ${ctx.new}`);
  return ctx.new;
}
```

```js title="Halve damage taken, keep healing as it is"
ctx => ctx.delta < 0 ? ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2 : ctx.new
```
